lessons.title: Reynolds number and laminar pipe flow

scenes.text: Thick crude oil moves smoothly in layers through a pipeline.
Reynolds number tells whether flow is laminar or turbulent.

steps.title: Reynolds number
steps.body: Re = ρVD/μ = VD/ν. Pipes: laminar Re < 2000, transitional 2000–4000, turbulent > 4000 (approximate).

steps.title: Hagen–Poiseuille (laminar, circular pipe)
steps.body:
Velocity profile parabolic: u = u_max(1 − r²/R²), u_max = 2V_avg.
Pressure drop Δp = 32μVL/D² ⇒ head loss h_f = 32μVL/(ρgD²).
Friction factor f = 64/Re (Darcy). Shear stress varies linearly from 0 at the centre to τ_w at the wall.
Between fixed parallel plates: u_max = 1.5 V_avg; Δp = 12μVL/t².

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** Oil μ = 0.1 Pa·s, ρ = 900, D = 0.1 m, V = 1 m/s: Re = 900 ⇒ laminar. Δp per 100 m = 32 × 0.1 × 1 × 100/0.01 = 32 kPa; h_f = 3.62 m.

**Example 2.** f = 64/900 = 0.0711 — check with Darcy: h_f = f(L/D)V²/2g = 0.0711 × 1000 × 1/19.62 = 3.62 m ✔.

**Example 3.** Water at 20 °C (ν = 10⁻⁶) in 25 mm pipe at 1 m/s: Re = 25 000 ⇒ turbulent.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using Fanning f (= f_Darcy/4) with the Darcy equation.
- Applying 64/Re to turbulent flow.
- Taking u_max = V_avg.

activity.prompt: Water ν = 1×10⁻⁶ m²/s, D = 0.05 m, V = 0.03 m/s. Reynolds number?

quiz.why: Pipe flow is laminar for Re below about 2000, and turbulent above about 4000. Between is the transition.
For laminar flow in a pipe, the Darcy friction factor is f = 64/Re. It depends only on Re and not on roughness.
The laminar profile in a pipe is a parabola, with maximum velocity at the centre equal to twice the average velocity.

quiz.q: Δp in laminar pipe flow is proportional to
quiz.why: By Hagen–Poiseuille, Δp = 32μLV/D², which is linear in V. In turbulent flow, it rises roughly as V².
Reynolds number is the ratio of inertial to viscous forces: Re = ρVD/μ = VD/ν.

scenes.text: A plumber chooses pipe sizes so the top floor still gets enough pressure.
Friction loss grows with V² — the Darcy–Weisbach equation.

steps.title: Major loss
steps.body:
h_f = fLV²/(2gD) (Darcy f). In terms of Q: h_f = 8fLQ²/(π²gD⁵) ≈ fLQ²/(12.1D⁵).
Friction factor: smooth pipes Blasius f = 0.316/Re^0.25 (Re < 10⁵); rough pipes depend on ε/D — Colebrook equation, Moody chart; fully rough f depends only on ε/D. Haaland explicit approximation: 1/√f = −1.8 log[(ε/3.7D)^1.11 + 6.9/Re].

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** Water 0.15 m pipe, 500 m long, V = 2 m/s, f = 0.02: h_f = 0.02 × 500 × 4/(19.62 × 0.15) = 13.6 m.

**Example 2.** Doubling the flow (same f) ⇒ h_f × 4 = 54.4 m.

**Example 3.** Halving the diameter at the same Q ⇒ h_f × 32 (∝ 1/D⁵).

steps.title: Quick sizing
steps.body: Because h_f ∝ 1/D⁵, a small increase in diameter hugely reduces losses — often cheaper than a bigger pump.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Fanning vs Darcy f confusion.
- Using the laminar formula in turbulent flow.
- Units of D in mm.

activity.prompt: h_f = fLV²/(2gD): f = 0.025, L = 200 m, V = 1.5 m/s, D = 0.1 m. h_f (m, 2 decimals)?

quiz.why: The Darcy–Weisbach equation gives the head loss due to friction in a pipe: h_f = fLV²/(2gD). The other formula with 32μ is for laminar flow only.

quiz.q: Halving D at same Q multiplies h_f by
quiz.why: For the same Q, V ∝ 1/D². Then h_f ∝ V²/D ∝ 1/D⁵. Halving D multiplies h_f by 2⁵ = 32.
The Blasius formula, f = 0.316/Re^0.25, is for smooth pipes in turbulent flow with Re up to about 10⁵. It does not apply to rough pipes or laminar flow.
The Moody chart gives the Darcy friction factor f for turbulent flow as a function of Reynolds number and relative roughness ε/D.
options: friction factor vs Re and ε/D

quiz.q: In fully rough turbulence f depends on
quiz.why: In the fully rough zone at high Re, the viscous sublayer is thinner than the roughness, so f depends only on relative roughness ε/D and no longer on Re.

story.title: Why many fittings slow the flow

scenes.text: A pipeline with many elbows and valves delivers less water.
Each fitting adds a minor loss K V²/2g.

steps.title: Minor losses
steps.body:
h_m = K V²/(2g).
- Sudden expansion: h = (V₁ − V₂)²/(2g) (Borda–Carnot).
- Sudden contraction: h ≈ 0.5 V₂²/(2g) (or (1/C_c − 1)²V₂²/2g).
- Pipe entrance (sharp) 0.5 V²/2g; exit to a tank 1.0 V²/2g.
- Elbows, valves: K from tables (e.g. globe valve open ≈ 10, gate valve open ≈ 0.2).
Equivalent length L_e = KD/f.

steps.title: HGL and EGL
steps.body: Energy grade line EGL = p/ρg + V²/2g + z; hydraulic grade line HGL = p/ρg + z (EGL − V²/2g). EGL slopes down by friction losses, drops at fittings, rises at pumps. Where HGL falls below the pipe, pressure is below atmospheric (siphons, cavitation risk).

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** Expansion from 0.1 m (V = 4 m/s) to 0.2 m (V = 1 m/s): h = 9/19.62 = 0.46 m.

**Example 2.** Two reservoirs joined by a 300 m, 0.2 m pipe, f = 0.02, with entrance (0.5) and exit (1.0): H = (0.5 + 1 + 0.02 × 300/0.2)V²/2g = 31.5 V²/2g. For H = 10 m: V = √(10 × 19.62/31.5) = 2.50 m/s; Q = 0.0785 m³/s.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Forgetting the exit loss (full velocity head).
- Using upstream velocity for contraction losses (use downstream).
- Drawing HGL above EGL.

activity.prompt: Sudden expansion: V₁ = 5 m/s to V₂ = 2 m/s. Head loss (m, 3 decimals)?

quiz.why: When a pipe discharges into a large reservoir, all the kinetic energy is lost, so the exit loss is V²/2g (K = 1).
For a sharp-edged pipe entrance from a reservoir, the loss coefficient is about 0.5, i.e. 0.5V²/2g. A well-rounded entrance gives about 0.04.
The energy grade line is above the hydraulic grade line by the velocity head: EGL − HGL = V²/2g.
The HGL is p/ρg + z. When it lies below the pipe, p/ρg is negative, so the pressure is below atmospheric. This is the case at siphon crests and risks cavitation.
For a sudden enlargement, the loss is (V₁ − V₂)²/2g (Borda–Carnot), from the momentum balance with the shock at the expansion.

lessons.title: Pipes in series and parallel; power transmission

scenes.text: A town's water flows through mains, branches and loops.
Series pipes add losses; parallel pipes share the same loss.

steps.title: Rules
steps.body:
**Series:** Q same; H = Σh_fᵢ (+ minor). Equivalent pipe (Dupuit): L_e/D_e⁵ = ΣLᵢ/Dᵢ⁵ (same f).
**Parallel:** h_f same in each branch; Q = ΣQᵢ.
**Power transmission through a pipe:** P = ρgQ(H − h_f); maximum when h_f = H/3 ⇒ η_max = 66.7%.
**Water hammer** (sudden valve closure): pressure rise Δp = ρcV (c = wave speed ≈ 1000–1400 m/s).

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** Series: 300 m of 0.3 m and 200 m of 0.2 m (f same) ⇒ equivalent 0.3 m pipe length: L_e = 300 + 200 × (0.3/0.2)⁵ = 300 + 1519 = 1819 m.

**Example 2.** Two parallel pipes of equal length and f, D₁ = 0.2, D₂ = 0.1: Q ∝ D^2.5 ⇒ Q₁/Q₂ = 2^2.5 = 5.66.

**Example 3.** Water hammer: V = 2 m/s stopped instantly, c = 1200 m/s: Δp = 1000 × 1200 × 2 = 2.4 MPa.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Adding flows in series or losses in parallel.
- Using D² instead of D⁵ in equivalent pipe.
- Closing valves too fast in long pipelines (water hammer damage).

activity.prompt: Series or parallel rule?

items.text: Same head loss in each pipe

quiz.q: Max power transmission efficiency through a pipe
quiz.why: For maximum power transmission through a pipe, the friction head loss is one third of the supply head: h_f = H/3. The efficiency is then (H − H/3)/H = 66.7%.
Pipes in parallel connect the same two junctions, so they share the same head loss, while the total flow splits between them.

quiz.q: Q ratio for parallel pipes D 2:1 (same L, f)
quiz.why: For equal head loss, h_f ∝ fLQ²/D⁵ gives Q ∝ D^2.5. The ratio is 2^2.5 = 5.66, so the larger pipe carries about 5.7 times as much.
The Joukowsky formula for pressure rise from sudden closure of a valve is Δp = ρcV, where c is the speed of pressure wave in the pipe.
The Dupuit equation for an equivalent pipe uses L/D⁵, because h_f ∝ fLQ²/D⁵ for the same discharge and friction factor.

questions.q: Turbulent pipe flow Re (approx.)
questions.why: Pipe flow is turbulent for Re above about 4000. Below 2000 it is laminar, and the range between is transitional.

questions.q: Friction loss in laminar flow ∝
questions.why: For laminar flow, the Hagen–Poiseuille law gives head loss proportional to the velocity V (not V²).

questions.q: Exit loss coefficient
questions.why: At exit to a large tank, the entire velocity head V²/2g is lost, so the exit loss coefficient is K = 1.

questions.q: f for laminar Re = 1600
questions.why: f = 64/Re = 64/1600 = 0.04 for laminar flow.

questions.q: Re for D = 0.2 m, V = 1 m/s, ν = 10⁻⁶
questions.why: Re = VD/ν = (1 × 0.2)/10⁻⁶ = 2×10⁵, so the flow is turbulent.

questions.q: h_f ratio if V doubles (same f)
questions.why: h_f = fLV²/(2gD), so with f, L, D fixed it is proportional to V². Doubling V gives 4 times the head loss.

questions.q: Assertion (A): Parallel pipes have equal head loss.  Reason (R): They connect the same two junctions whose energy levels are fixed.
options: Both A and R are true, and R correctly explains A
Both A and R are true, but R does not explain A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
questions.why: Both are true. The two junctions of parallel pipes each have one energy level, so the head loss from one to the other is the same for every path. R explains A.

questions.q: Laminar Δp: μ 0.05 Pa·s, V 0.5 m/s, L 50 m, D 0.05 m
Expansion 0.05 → 0.1 m, V₁ = 4 m/s: loss
questions.why: By continuity, V₂ = V₁(A₁/A₂) = 4 × (1/4) = 1 m/s. Loss = (V₁ − V₂)²/2g = 9/19.62 ≈ 0.459 m.

questions.q: Reservoirs 15 m apart, pipe 400 m, D 0.25 m, f 0.02, K_entrance 0.5, exit 1: V
Case: A 2 km pipeline (D 0.3 m) carries 0.1 m³/s with f = 0.018. Head loss
Equivalent length of 100 m of 0.1 m pipe in terms of 0.2 m pipe
questions.why: For the same friction loss, equivalent length ∝ D⁵. 100 m of 0.1 m pipe equals 100 × (0.2/0.1)⁵ = 100 × 32 = 3200 m of 0.2 m pipe.

questions.q: Water hammer for V = 1.5 m/s, c = 1400 m/s
questions.why: Δp = ρcV = 1000 × 1400 × 1.5 = 2.1×10⁶ Pa = 2.1 MPa. This is a large pressure surge from sudden valve closure.

questions.q: Power through pipe: H = 60 m, h_f = 20 m, Q = 0.5 m³/s
Wall shear stress in laminar flow relates to Δp by
questions.why: A force balance on a fluid cylinder of length L gives Δp × πD²/4 = τ_w × πDL, so τ_w = ΔpD/(4L).

courses.title: Fluid Mechanics · Unit 4 · Dimensional analysis, boundary layer and turbomachines
courses.summary: Dimensional homogeneity, Rayleigh and Buckingham π methods, dimensionless numbers and model similitude, boundary-layer concepts (thicknesses, laminar/turbulent, separation), drag and lift, and introduction to hydraulic turbines and centrifugal pumps (heads, efficiencies, specific speed).
outcomes: Form dimensionless groups with Buckingham π
Apply Reynolds and Froude model laws
Estimate boundary-layer thickness and drag
Compute pump/turbine power, efficiency and specific speed
courses.note: topic order may differ by edition

scenes.text: Naval architects test a 1:25 scale model in a towing tank.
Dimensional analysis tells how to scale the results.

steps.title: Method
steps.body:
Dimensions M, L, T. A physically correct equation is dimensionally homogeneous.
**Buckingham π theorem:** n variables with m fundamental dimensions ⇒ n − m independent dimensionless π groups. Choose m repeating variables (geometry, flow, fluid property — e.g. D, V, ρ) that together contain all dimensions and don't form a π themselves.

steps.title: Common dimensionless numbers
steps.body:
- Reynolds Re = ρVL/μ (inertia/viscous)
- Froude Fr = V/√(gL) (inertia/gravity) — free-surface flows
- Euler Eu = Δp/(ρV²)
- Weber We = ρV²L/σ (surface tension)
- Mach Ma = V/c (compressibility)

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** Drag F on a sphere depends on D, V, ρ, μ: n = 5, m = 3 ⇒ 2 groups: F/(ρV²D²) = φ(ρVD/μ).

**Example 2.** Pipe pressure drop Δp = f(D, L, V, ρ, μ, ε): 7 − 3 = 4 groups: Δp/(ρV²), L/D, Re, ε/D.

**Example 3.** Dimensions of μ: [ML⁻¹T⁻¹]; of power: [ML²T⁻³].

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Choosing repeating variables that include the dependent variable.
- Choosing repeating variables that are dimensionally dependent (e.g. D and L together).
- Wrong number of groups.

activity.prompt: Variables 6, fundamental dimensions 3. Number of π groups?

quiz.why: Viscosity μ has units Pa·s = (N/m²)·s, which in base dimensions is ML⁻¹T⁻¹. The form L²T⁻¹ is for kinematic viscosity.
The Froude number is Fr = V/√(gL), the ratio of inertial to gravity forces. Mach is V/c and Reynolds is ρVL/μ.

quiz.q: Number of π groups for n = 7, m = 3
quiz.why: By the Buckingham π theorem, the number of dimensionless groups = n − m = 7 − 3 = 4, where n is the number of variables and m the number of fundamental dimensions.
Repeating variables must not include the dependent variable, because it should appear in only one π group. They should also be dimensionally independent.
The Mach number (V/c) matters when compressibility is significant, i.e. in high-speed gas flow, near or above about Mach 0.3.

scenes.text: A dam spillway is tested at 1:50 scale in a lab.
Froude similarity sets the model velocity and discharge.

steps.title: Similarity
steps.body:
Geometric (shape, length ratio L_r), kinematic (velocity ratios), dynamic (force ratios equal ⇒ key π equal).
**Reynolds model law** (pipes, submerged bodies, aircraft at low Ma): (VL/ν)_m = (VL/ν)_p.
**Froude model law** (spillways, ships, open channels): V_r = √L_r, Q_r = L_r^2.5, T_r = √L_r, F_r = L_r³ (same fluid).
Distorted models use different horizontal and vertical scales (rivers).

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** Spillway 1:50, prototype Q = 1000 m³/s ⇒ model Q = 1000/50^2.5 = 1000/17 678 = 0.0566 m³/s.

**Example 2.** Model velocity 1 m/s ⇒ prototype 1 × √50 = 7.07 m/s.

**Example 3.** Reynolds law: car 1:5 model in same air ⇒ V_m = 5V_p (often impractical — use wind tunnels with high speeds or pressurised tunnels).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using Reynolds scaling for free-surface flows.
- Forgetting Q ratio exponent 2.5 (Froude).
- Expecting to satisfy Re and Fr simultaneously with the same fluid (generally impossible).

activity.prompt: Froude model 1:25, model velocity 0.8 m/s. Prototype velocity (m/s)?

quiz.why: Ship and spillway models involve a free surface, where gravity dominates. So they use Froude similarity.
With Froude scaling, V_r = √L_r and area A_r = L_r², so Q_r = V_rA_r = L_r^(1/2) × L_r² = L_r^2.5.
In pressurised pipe flow, viscous forces dominate, not gravity, so Reynolds similarity is used for the models.
Dynamic similarity needs the ratios of all the relevant forces (the π groups, such as Re and Fr) to be equal for model and prototype, along with geometric and kinematic similarity.
With Froude scaling, time ratio T_r = L_r/V_r = L_r/√L_r = √L_r.

scenes.text: Dimpled golf balls fly farther than smooth ones.
Dimples trip the boundary layer to turbulence, delaying separation and cutting pressure drag.

steps.title: Boundary layer on a flat plate
steps.body:
Thickness δ (99% of U). Laminar (Blasius): δ/x = 5/√Re_x; C_f(avg) = 1.328/√Re_L. Turbulent (1/7 power law): δ/x = 0.37/Re_x^0.2; C_f = 0.074/Re_L^0.2. Transition around Re_x ≈ 5×10⁵.
Displacement thickness δ* (laminar δ/3 for linear… Blasius δ* = 1.72x/√Re_x), momentum thickness θ.
**Separation:** occurs in adverse pressure gradient (dp/dx > 0) when wall shear becomes zero ⇒ wake and pressure drag.

steps.title: Drag and lift
steps.body: F_D = C_D(½ρV²)A; F_L = C_L(½ρV²)A. Streamlined bodies: mostly skin-friction drag; bluff bodies: mostly pressure (form) drag. Sphere C_D ≈ 0.47 (subcritical); drag crisis near Re ≈ 3×10⁵ where C_D drops. Stokes' law (Re < 1): F_D = 3πμVD ⇒ terminal velocity of small particles V_t = (ρ_s − ρ)gD²/(18μ).

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** Air (ν = 1.5×10⁻⁵) over a plate at 3 m/s, x = 1 m: Re = 2×10⁵ (laminar) ⇒ δ = 5/447 = 11.2 mm.

**Example 2.** Car C_D = 0.3, A = 2 m², 30 m/s, ρ = 1.2: F_D = 0.3 × 0.5 × 1.2 × 900 × 2 = 324 N; power = 9.7 kW.

**Example 3.** Sand grain 0.1 mm (ρ_s 2650) settling in water (μ 0.001): V_t = 1650 × 9.81 × 10⁻⁸/0.018 = 9.0 mm/s (Re ≈ 0.9, Stokes OK).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using laminar formulas beyond transition.
- Using the wrong reference area for C_D.
- Applying Stokes' law at Re ≫ 1.

activity.prompt: Car: C_D 0.32, A 2.2 m², ρ 1.2, V 25 m/s. Drag force (N, nearest whole)?

quiz.why: For laminar flow over a flat plate (Blasius solution), the boundary layer thickness is δ = 5x/√Re_x.
Separation occurs when the boundary layer moves against an adverse pressure gradient (pressure rising downstream), which slows the near-wall fluid until it reverses.
For bluff bodies, the separated wake gives a large pressure difference between the front and back, so most of the drag is pressure (form) drag, not skin friction.
Stokes' law for a sphere in creeping flow (Re < 1): drag F = 3πμVD.
Dimples trip the boundary layer into turbulence, which sticks to the ball longer and delays separation. This shrinks the wake and reduces drag.

scenes.text: A hydro plant with 300 m head uses Pelton wheels; a low-head river plant uses Kaplan turbines.
Specific speed picks the right machine.

steps.title: Turbines
steps.body:
Power available P = ρgQH; η_o = shaft power/(ρgQH) = η_h × η_m.
Types: **Pelton** (impulse, high head, low specific speed); **Francis** (reaction, medium head); **Kaplan** (axial reaction, low head, high specific speed, adjustable blades).
Specific speed N_s = N√P/H^(5/4) (P in kW, H in m, N in rpm): Pelton ~10–35 (single jet), Francis ~60–300, Kaplan ~300–1000.
Pelton jet velocity V = C_v√(2gH); optimum bucket speed u ≈ 0.46V.

steps.title: Centrifugal pumps
steps.body: Manometric head H_m; power input = ρgQH_m/η_o. Specific speed N_s = N√Q/H^(3/4). Priming needed (displace air). **Cavitation:** local pressure below vapour pressure ⇒ bubbles collapse, damage — keep NPSH available > NPSH required. Affinity laws (same pump): Q ∝ N, H ∝ N², P ∝ N³. Series pumps add head; parallel add flow.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Mixing turbine (P-based) and pump (Q-based) specific speeds.
- Running pumps dry (no priming).
- Ignoring NPSH ⇒ cavitation damage.

quiz.why: By the affinity laws, H ∝ N², so doubling the speed multiplies the head by 4 (Q ∝ N, P ∝ N³).

questions.why: The Reynolds number is the ratio of inertial forces to viscous forces. A large Re means inertia dominates and flow tends towards turbulence.

questions.why: Pelton turbines are impulse machines used for high heads (hundreds of metres) and low flows, such as in mountain plants.

questions.q: Pumps must be primed because
questions.why: A centrifugal pump gives a pressure rise proportional to the fluid density. Air is so light that the pump cannot create enough suction, so it must be primed with water.

Both A and R are true, but R does not explain A
A is true, but R is false

lessons.title: Stress, strain and Hooke's law

scenes.text: A steel crane hook carries 50 kN.
Is it safe? Stress = load/area, compared with the allowable stress.

steps.title: Definitions
steps.body:
Normal stress σ = P/A; strain ε = δL/L; Hooke's law σ = Eε ⇒ δL = PL/(AE). Shear stress τ = F/A; shear strain γ; τ = Gγ.
Poisson's ratio ν = −lateral strain/longitudinal strain (steel ≈ 0.3). Volumetric strain (bar) e_v = ε(1 − 2ν).
Factor of safety = failure (yield/ultimate) stress/working stress.

steps.title: Stress–strain diagram (mild steel)
steps.body: Proportional limit → elastic limit → upper and lower yield points → strain hardening → ultimate stress → necking → fracture. Ductile materials show large plastic strain (% elongation); brittle materials (cast iron) fracture with little deformation. Proof stress (0.2% offset) for materials without a clear yield point (aluminium).

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** Steel rod 20 mm dia, 2 m long, 50 kN, E = 200 GPa: A = 314.2 mm²; σ = 159.2 MPa; δ = 50 000 × 2000/(314.2 × 200 000) = 1.59 mm.

**Example 2.** Same rod lateral strain with ν = 0.3: ε = 7.96×10⁻⁴ ⇒ lateral −2.39×10⁻⁴ ⇒ diameter decreases by 0.0048 mm.

**Example 3.** Ultimate 420 MPa, FoS 3 ⇒ allowable 140 MPa.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Units: N/mm² = MPa; E in GPa = 10³ N/mm².
- Using diameter instead of area.
- Applying Hooke's law beyond the proportional limit.

activity.prompt: Steel bar: P = 100 kN, A = 500 mm², L = 1000 mm, E = 200 GPa. Elongation (mm)?

quiz.why: Hooke's law says that within the elastic limit stress is proportional to strain: σ = Eε, where E is Young's modulus.
1 MPa = 10⁶ N/m² = 1 N/mm², since 1 m² = 10⁶ mm².
Poisson's ratio is the ratio of lateral to longitudinal strain. Steel is about 0.3, and the usual range for metals is 0.25–0.35.
Materials like aluminium have no distinct yield point. So the proof stress (such as the 0.2% offset stress) is used as the practical yield strength.
options: materials without a clear yield point

quiz.why: Elongation of an axially loaded bar is δ = PL/(AE): load times length divided by area times modulus.

lessons.title: Elastic constants and their relations

scenes.text: Rubber is nearly incompressible (ν ≈ 0.5); cork has ν ≈ 0 — ideal for bottle stoppers.
E, G, K and ν are linked for isotropic materials.

steps.title: Relations (isotropic)
steps.body:
E = 2G(1 + ν); E = 3K(1 − 2ν); E = 9KG/(3K + G).
−1 < ν ≤ 0.5 (most materials 0–0.5); ν = 0.5 ⇒ incompressible (K → ∞).
Volumetric strain under triaxial stress: e_v = (σₓ + σ_y + σ_z)(1 − 2ν)/E; hydrostatic pressure p: e_v = −p/K.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** E = 200 GPa, ν = 0.3: G = 76.9 GPa; K = 166.7 GPa.

**Example 2.** E = 210 GPa, G = 80 GPa ⇒ ν = E/(2G) − 1 = 0.3125.

**Example 3.** Steel cube 100 mm under 50 MPa hydrostatic pressure (K = 166.7 GPa): e_v = −3×10⁻⁴ ⇒ ΔV = −300 mm³.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using E = 2G(1 − ν).
- Claiming ν > 0.5 for isotropic solids.
- Sign of volumetric strain under compression.

activity.prompt: Relation

quiz.why: The bulk modulus K = E/(3(1 − 2ν)) must be positive, so ν < 0.5. Rubber-like incompressible materials come close to 0.5.
An isotropic elastic material has only 2 independent constants. Others (like G, K) follow from any two, such as E and ν.
Cork does not expand sideways when compressed, which is why it fits bottle necks. So its Poisson's ratio is about 0.

lessons.title: Varying sections, compound bars and thermal stresses

scenes.text: Old railway tracks had gaps between rails.
Without them, restrained thermal expansion would cause huge compressive stress and buckling.

steps.title: Key results
steps.body:
Stepped bar: δ = (P/E)ΣLᵢ/Aᵢ. Tapered circular bar (d₁ to d₂): δ = 4PL/(πEd₁d₂).
Compound bar (two materials sharing load, same strain): P = σ₁A₁ + σ₂A₂, σ₁/E₁ = σ₂/E₂.
Thermal: free expansion δ = αLΔT; fully restrained stress σ = EαΔT. Compound bar heated: steel–copper — copper (higher α) in compression, steel in tension, with force equilibrium σ_sA_s = σ_cA_c and compatibility.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** Steel rail α = 12×10⁻⁶ /°C, ΔT = 40 °C, fully restrained: σ = 200 000 × 12×10⁻⁶ × 40 = 96 MPa (compression).

**Example 2.** Concrete column 300 × 300 mm with 4 bars of 20 mm (A_s = 1257 mm²), m = E_s/E_c = 15, load 1000 kN: A_c = 88 743; σ_c(A_c + mA_s) = 10⁶ ⇒ σ_c = 10⁶/(88 743 + 18 855) = 9.29 MPa; σ_s = 139.4 MPa.

**Example 3.** Tapered bar d 40 → 20 mm, L = 1 m, P = 50 kN, E = 200 GPa: δ = 4 × 50 000 × 1000/(π × 200 000 × 800) = 0.398 mm.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Adding elongations of parallel members (they have equal strain).
- Using gross area including steel for concrete.
- Forgetting thermal stress is independent of length.

activity.prompt: Restrained steel bar heated 50 °C (α 12×10⁻⁶/°C, E 200 GPa). Thermal stress (MPa)?

quiz.q: Thermal stress in a restrained bar
quiz.why: If a bar is fully restrained, the thermal strain α ΔT is prevented, giving stress σ = EαΔT. It is compressive on heating.

quiz.q: Compound bar members share the same
quiz.why: In a compound bar, the members are joined and extend together, so they have the same strain (compatibility). Their stresses differ in proportion to E.
For a tapered circular bar, the extension is δ = 4PL/(πE d₁d₂), where d₁ and d₂ are the end diameters. If d₁ = d₂ it reduces to PL/(AE).
σ = EαΔT has no length term. The free expansion αLΔT depends on the length, but the stress to prevent it does not.

quiz.q: In a heated steel–copper compound bar, copper is in
quiz.why: Copper has the larger α, so it wants to expand more than steel, but the steel restrains it. So copper is in compression and steel in tension.

lessons.title: Strain energy and impact loading

scenes.text: Dropping a load onto a rope stresses it far more than lowering it gently.
A suddenly applied load doubles the stress of a gradual one.

steps.title: Strain energy
steps.body:
U = ½Pδ = σ²V/(2E) (resilience). Proof resilience = σ_p²V/(2E); modulus of resilience σ_p²/(2E).
- Gradual load: σ = P/A.
- Sudden load: σ = 2P/A.
- Impact (weight W falling height h): σ = (W/A)[1 + √(1 + 2AEh/(WL))]; if h ≫ δ: σ ≈ √(2EWh/(AL)).
Shear strain energy: τ²V/(2G).

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** Bar A = 500 mm², L = 2 m, E = 200 GPa, gradual load 50 kN: σ = 100 MPa; U = 100² × (10⁶ mm³)/(2 × 200 000) = 25 000 N·mm = 25 J.

**Example 2.** Same load suddenly applied: σ = 200 MPa.

**Example 3.** 1 kN falling 100 mm onto a collar of the same bar: σ = 2[1 + √(1 + 2 × 500 × 200 000 × 100/(1000 × 2000))] = 2[1 + √(10 001)] = 2 × 101 = 202 MPa.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Treating a sudden load as gradual.
- Units in the impact formula (keep N and mm).
- Forgetting strain energy depends on σ², so stress concentrations matter greatly.

activity.prompt: Load 20 kN applied suddenly to a bar of area 400 mm². Stress (MPa)?

quiz.q: Sudden load stress factor vs gradual
quiz.why: For a suddenly applied load P, the work done is P·δ and the strain energy stored is ½P_eδ. Equating gives P_e = 2P, so the stress is twice that for the same load applied gradually (factor 2).
Strain energy per unit volume = ½ × stress × strain = ½σ(σ/E) = σ²/(2E).
Proof resilience is the maximum strain energy that can be stored in a body without permanent deformation, i.e. at the elastic limit.
The stress from a falling weight depends on the fall height, the weight, and the bar's stiffness (A, E, L). A higher fall or a stiffer bar gives more stress.
U = ½Pδ assumes the load rises gradually from zero, with the bar elastic. For sudden or impact loads, the work done is different.

sources: Standard Strength of Materials syllabus (ME/CE core)

RCC column: σ_c if σ_s = 120 MPa, m = 15
questions.why: In a composite (RCC) column, strains are equal: σ_s/E_s = σ_c/E_c, so σ_c = σ_s/m = 120/15 = 8 MPa.

questions.q: Compound bar steel (A 1000, E 200) + copper (A 1000, E 100) carries 300 kN: σ_steel
questions.why: The two members share the same strain, so σ_s/200 = σ_c/100, giving σ_s = 2σ_c. Load: 1000(σ_s + σ_c) = 300 000, so 3σ_c = 300, σ_c = 100 and σ_s = 200 MPa.

questions.q: Case: A 30 m rail is laid at 15 °C with no gap. On a 55 °C day, stress (α 12×10⁻⁶, E 200 GPa)
questions.why: The rail is prevented from expanding, so σ = EαΔT = 200 000 × 12×10⁻⁶ × 40 = 96 MPa. A heated, restrained bar is in compression. The length does not matter.

questions.q: Volumetric strain of a bar ε = 10⁻³, ν = 0.25
questions.why: Volumetric strain = ε(1 − 2ν) = 10⁻³ × (1 − 0.5) = 5×10⁻⁴. The lateral contraction reduces the volume gain.

questions.q: Modulus of resilience for σ_p = 250 MPa, E = 200 GPa
questions.why: Modulus of resilience = σ_p²/(2E) = 250²/(2 × 200 000) = 62 500/400 000 ≈ 0.156 N·mm/mm³ (MPa).

lessons.title: Conventions and cantilevers

scenes.text: A balcony projects from a building like a cantilever.
The bending moment is largest at the wall — that's where it would crack.

steps.title: Conventions
steps.body: Shear force at a section: sum of vertical forces on one side (left-up positive, 'clockwise' shear positive). Bending moment: sum of moments on one side — sagging positive, hogging negative.

steps.title: Cantilever results (free end at x = 0, fixed at x = L)
steps.body:
- Point load W at free end: SF = W (constant), BM = −Wx, max −WL at the fixed end.
- UDL w over full span: SF = wx (linear), BM = −wx²/2, max −wL²/2.
- UVL zero at free end to w at fixed end: SF = wx²/(2L), BM = −wx³/(6L), max −wL²/6.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** 3 m cantilever, 10 kN at the free end: M_max = −30 kN·m at the support.

**Example 2.** 2 m cantilever with 5 kN/m UDL: V_max = 10 kN, M_max = −10 kN·m.

**Example 3.** Both loads together (superposition): M_support = −30 − 5 × 9/2 (if 3 m span with UDL) = −52.5 kN·m.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Sign of BM for cantilevers (hogging = negative).
- Taking UDL moment with full length instead of half (centroid at L/2).
- Forgetting the UVL resultant acts at one-third from the larger end.

activity.prompt: Cantilever 4 m with UDL 3 kN/m. Maximum bending moment magnitude (kN·m)?

quiz.q: Cantilever with end load: max BM at
quiz.why: For a cantilever with an end load, the moment is load × distance from the load. It is largest at the fixed end, where the lever arm is the longest.
A cantilever of length L with a UDL has a resultant wL at L/2 from the support, so M = wL × L/2 = wL²/2 at the fixed end.
By the usual convention, a sagging bending moment (beam curving like a smile) is positive, and hogging is negative.

quiz.q: SFD for cantilever with end point load is
quiz.why: For a cantilever with a point load at the end, the shear force equals the load at every section, so the SFD is a constant rectangle.
Under a UDL, the shear force varies linearly. The bending moment is the integral of the shear force, so the BMD is a parabola.

sources: Standard Strength of Materials syllabus (ME/CE core)

lessons.title: Simply supported beams

scenes.text: A wooden floor beam rests on two walls and carries furniture.
Maximum bending moment occurs where shear force changes sign.

steps.title: Standard results (span L)
steps.body:
- Central point load W: R = W/2, M_max = WL/4 at centre.
- Point load W at a from A (b from B): R_A = Wb/L, M_max = Wab/L under the load.
- Full UDL w: R = wL/2, M_max = wL²/8 at centre; SF zero at centre.
- UVL zero at A to w at B: R_A = wL/6, R_B = wL/3; M_max = wL²/(9√3) at x = L/√3 from A.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** 6 m beam, 12 kN at 2 m from A: R_A = 8, R_B = 4; M_max = 12 × 2 × 4/6 = 16 kN·m.

**Example 2.** 8 m beam, UDL 2 kN/m: M_max = 2 × 64/8 = 16 kN·m.

**Example 3.** 6 m beam, UDL 4 kN/m over left half only: R_A = 12 × 4.5/6 = 9 kN, R_B = 3 kN. Zero shear at x = 9/4 = 2.25 m ⇒ M_max = 9 × 2.25 − 4 × 2.25²/2 = 10.125 kN·m.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Assuming M_max is always at mid-span (only for symmetric loading).
- Missing jumps in SFD at point loads.
- Using total UDL in moment calculations without its lever arm.

activity.prompt: Simply supported 10 m beam with UDL 4 kN/m. M_max (kN·m)?

quiz.why: For a simply supported beam with a central point load, M_max = WL/4 at mid-span. For example, W = 8 kN and L = 4 m gives 8 kN·m.
For a simply supported beam with a full UDL, M_max = wL²/8 at mid-span. The cantilever value of wL²/2 is four times larger.
Since dM/dx = V, the moment is at a maximum or minimum where the shear force is zero and changes sign.

quiz.q: Point load at 2 m on a 5 m span (W = 10): R_A
quiz.why: Take moments about B: R_A = W × b/L = 10 × 3/5 = 6 kN, where b is the distance from the load to the far support (5 − 2 = 3 m).
The SFD under a UDL is linear since the shear changes at the constant rate w along the beam.

sources: Standard Strength of Materials syllabus (ME/CE core)

lessons.title: Overhanging beams and contraflexure

scenes.text: Bridge decks often overhang their piers.
Moments change sign along the beam — at the point of contraflexure.

steps.title: Approach
steps.body: Find reactions from equilibrium; draw SFD section by section; BM sagging between supports may become hogging over the overhang. **Point of contraflexure:** where BM = 0 and changes sign (not at a free end). Reinforcement and splices are placed with this in mind.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** Beam AB = 6 m simply supported with overhang BC = 2 m; UDL 2 kN/m over the whole 8 m.
ΣM_A: R_B × 6 = 16 × 4 ⇒ R_B = 10.667 kN; R_A = 5.333 kN.
M_B = −2 × 2²/2 = −4 kN·m. Between A and B: M(x) = 5.333x − x². Zero shear at x = 2.667 ⇒ M_max = 7.11 kN·m.
Contraflexure: 5.333x − x² = 0 ⇒ x = 5.333 m from A.

**Example 2.** Overhanging both sides symmetrically — two contraflexure points, symmetric about the centre.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Calling the free end a contraflexure point (BM is zero but doesn't change sign).
- Ignoring the hogging moment at the support.
- Sign errors in reactions for overhangs (one may be small or even negative).

activity.prompt: Drawing SFD and BMD
items: Find support reactions using equilibrium
Divide the beam at loads and supports
Compute SF at key points (jumps at point loads)
Find BM at key points and where SF = 0
Sketch curves (linear/parabolic) and mark max BM and contraflexure

quiz.why: A point of contraflexure is where the bending moment changes sign, passing through zero, so the beam changes between sagging and hogging.

quiz.q: BM at the overhang support (2 m, UDL 2 kN/m)
quiz.why: For an overhang of a = 2 m carrying UDL w = 2 kN/m, the moment at the support is −wa²/2 = −2 × 4/2 = −4 kN·m. It is negative since the overhang hogs.
This refers to a worked example in the lesson. The maximum sagging moment, found where the shear force is zero, comes to about 7.11 kN·m.
This refers to a worked example in the lesson. The point of contraflexure is where M changes sign, which is found by setting M = 0 and gives 5.333 m from A.
Overhanging beams have hogging moment over the support, and sagging moment between supports. So there are both, with points of contraflexure between them.

sources: Standard Strength of Materials syllabus (ME/CE core)

lessons.title: Load–shear–moment relations

scenes.text: Design software outputs SFD/BMD — engineers sanity-check them by hand.
The slope of the BMD equals the shear force.

steps.title: Relations
steps.body:
dV/dx = −w (load intensity downward positive); dM/dx = V.
⇒ Change in SF between two sections = −(area of load diagram); change in BM = area of SF diagram.
- No load: V constant, M linear.
- UDL: V linear, M parabolic.
- UVL: V parabolic, M cubic.
- Point load: jump in V, kink in M.
- Applied couple: jump in M (V unchanged).

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** SF diagram area from A to the zero-shear point (triangle with base 2.667 and height 5.333) = 7.11 ⇒ M_max ✔ (Example in previous lesson).

**Example 2.** Simply supported 4 m beam with a clockwise couple 8 kN·m at mid-span: R_A = −2 kN, R_B = +2 kN (pair); BM jumps by 8 kN·m at the centre: from −4 to +4 kN·m.

**Example 3.** SF constant at 10 kN over 3 m ⇒ BM changes by 30 kN·m.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Forgetting the jump in BMD under an applied couple.
- Wrong sign of dV/dx = −w (convention dependent — be consistent).
- Using these relations across a point load without accounting for the jump.

activity.prompt: Load type → BMD shape

items.text: Simply supported beam with full UDL

quiz.why: The relation between moment and shear is dM/dx = V, so the slope of the bending moment diagram equals the shear force.

quiz.q: Change in BM between two points =
quiz.why: Integrating dM/dx = V, the change in bending moment between two points equals the area under the shear force diagram between them.

quiz.q: Applied couple causes a jump in
quiz.why: A concentrated couple applied to a beam produces a sudden jump in the bending moment diagram. The shear force diagram is unchanged. A point load makes a jump in the SFD.

quiz.q: Under a UVL, the SFD is
quiz.why: Under a uniformly varying load, the shear force is the integral of a linear load, so the SFD is parabolic (and the BMD is cubic).

quiz.q: SF constant 5 kN over 4 m ⇒ ΔM
quiz.why: The change in moment = area of the SFD = 5 kN × 4 m = 20 kN·m.

sources: Standard Strength of Materials syllabus (ME/CE core)

questions.q: BM at free end of a cantilever
questions.why: At the free end of a cantilever there is no load beyond that point, so the bending moment is zero there.

questions.q: SF jumps at
questions.why: Shear force jumps in value at concentrated (point) loads and reactions, equal to the size of the load. It changes gradually under UDLs.

questions.q: M_max central point load 8 kN on 4 m span
questions.why: M_max = WL/4 = 8 × 4/4 = 8 kN·m, at mid-span.

questions.q: Cantilever 2 m, end load 5 kN and UDL 2 kN/m: M at support
questions.why: At the support: end load 5 × 2 = 10 kN·m plus UDL 2 × 2²/2 = 4 kN·m, giving 14 kN·m. It is hogging, so −14 kN·m.

questions.q: Simply supported 6 m, loads 10 kN at 2 m and 10 kN at 4 m: M_max
questions.why: By symmetry, each reaction is 10 kN. The moment at 2 m is 10 × 2 = 20 kN·m, and it stays constant between the loads, so M_max = 20 kN·m.

questions.q: UVL 0 → w on simply supported span L: R_B (heavy end)
questions.why: The total load is wL/2 acting at L/3 from the heavy end. Taking moments, the reaction at the heavy end is (wL/2) × (2/3) = wL/3, and at the light end it is wL/6.

questions.q: Assertion (A): Maximum bending moment occurs where shear force is zero.  Reason (R): dM/dx = V, so M is stationary where V = 0.
options: Both A and R are true, and R correctly explains A
Both A and R are true, but R does not explain A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
questions.why: Both are true. Since dM/dx = V, the moment has a stationary (maximum or minimum) value where V = 0. R explains A.

questions.q: 6 m beam, 18 kN at 2 m from A: M_max
questions.why: R_A = 18 × 4/6 = 12 kN (load is 2 m from A, 4 m from B). M at the load = 12 × 2 = 24 kN·m. The maximum is under the load.

questions.q: Cantilever 3 m with UVL 0 at free end to 6 kN/m at support: M_max
questions.why: For a cantilever carrying a triangular load that is zero at the free end and w at the support, the total load is wL/2 = 9 kN acting at L/3 = 1 m from the support. M = 9 × 1 = 9 kN·m (wL²/6).

questions.q: Beam 8 m, UDL 3 kN/m on left 4 m: R_A
questions.why: The UDL's resultant is 3 × 4 = 12 kN, acting 2 m from A. R_A = 12 × (8 − 2)/8 = 12 × 6/8 = 9 kN.

questions.q: Position of zero shear for that beam (from A)
questions.why: Shear at x from A (within the UDL) = 9 − 3x. Setting it to zero gives x = 3 m, where the bending moment is maximum.

questions.q: Case: A 10 m footbridge (simply supported) carries 2 kN/m dead load plus a 10 kN person-cart at mid-span. M_max
questions.why: UDL: wL²/8 = 2 × 10²/8 = 25 kN·m; central point load: WL/4 = 10 × 10/4 = 25 kN·m. Both maxima occur at mid-span, so M_max = 25 + 25 = 50 kN·m.

questions.q: Overhanging beam AB = 4 m, BC = 1 m, point load 10 kN at C: BM at B
questions.why: The overhang BC carries a 10 kN load at 1 m from B, so M_B = −10 × 1 = −10 kN·m. The sign is negative since it is hogging.

questions.q: UVL max BM on simply supported span (0 → w)
questions.why: For a UVL (0 to w) on a simply supported beam, the maximum moment is at x = L/√3 and equals wL²/(9√3) ≈ 0.064wL².

questions.q: Couple 12 kN·m at mid-span of a 6 m simply supported beam: reactions
questions.why: A couple M on a simply supported beam is balanced by a pair of equal and opposite reactions: R = M/L = 12/6 = 2 kN, one up and one down.

courses.title: Strength of Materials · Unit 3 · Bending stresses, shear stresses and torsion
courses.summary: Theory of simple bending, flexure formula, section modulus, stress distribution in rectangular, circular and I-sections, shear stress distribution in beams, and torsion of solid and hollow circular shafts with power transmission.
outcomes: Apply M/I = σ/y = E/R
Compute section modulus and choose economical sections
Find shear stress distribution and maxima
Design solid and hollow shafts for torque and power
courses.note: topic order may differ by edition

lessons.title: Theory of simple bending

scenes.text: Steel beams are I-shaped: flanges far from the neutral axis carry most of the bending stress.
The flexure formula explains why.

steps.title: Flexure formula
steps.body:
Assumptions: plane sections remain plane, linear elastic, homogeneous, pure bending, symmetric section.
M/I = σ/y = E/R. Neutral axis passes through the centroid (zero stress). σ_max = M/Z, Z = I/y_max (section modulus).
- Rectangle: Z = bd²/6
- Solid circle: Z = πd³/32
- Hollow circle: Z = π(D⁴ − d⁴)/(32D)

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** Rectangular beam 100 × 200 mm, M = 20 kN·m: Z = 100 × 200²/6 = 666 667 mm³; σ_max = 20×10⁶/666 667 = 30 MPa.

**Example 2.** Solid shaft d = 100 mm as a beam, M = 5 kN·m: Z = 98 175 mm³; σ = 50.9 MPa.

**Example 3.** Radius of curvature: E = 200 GPa, y = 10 mm, σ = 100 MPa ⇒ R = Ey/σ = 20 m.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using d³ vs d² wrongly in Z of a rectangle.
- Taking y from the bottom instead of from the neutral axis.
- Applying the formula to unsymmetrical sections about non-principal axes.

activity.prompt: Rectangular beam b = 150 mm, d = 300 mm, M = 45 kN·m. Max bending stress (MPa)?

quiz.why: The flexure formula for pure bending is M/I = σ/y = E/R, linking bending moment, stress and radius of curvature.
In bending, the stress is proportional to the distance y from the neutral axis (σ = My/I). At the neutral axis y = 0, so the bending stress is zero.
For a rectangle, I = bd³/12 and y_max = d/2, so Z = I/y_max = bd²/6.
For a solid circle, I = πd⁴/64 and y_max = d/2, so Z = I/y_max = πd³/32.

quiz.q: For the same area, the most efficient beam section in bending
quiz.why: For the same material area, an I-section puts most of the area in the flanges, far from the neutral axis. That gives a larger I and Z, so it is the most efficient in bending.

sources: Standard Strength of Materials syllabus (ME/CE core)

lessons.title: Bending stress in composite and practical sections

scenes.text: An engineer picks a rolled steel joist from a handbook by its section modulus.
Required Z = M_max/σ_allow.

steps.title: Design use
steps.body:
Required Z = M_max/σ_allow. For a given depth, deeper sections are much stronger (Z ∝ d²). Strength of a beam ∝ Z; stiffness ∝ I.
Unsymmetric sections (T, channel): find the centroid first; y_max differs for top and bottom fibres ⇒ different stresses (compression/tension).

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** Simply supported 6 m beam with UDL 10 kN/m: M = 45 kN·m; σ_allow = 165 MPa ⇒ Z_req = 272 727 mm³ ⇒ choose a rolled section with Z ≥ 273 cm³.

**Example 2.** T-section (flange 100 × 20, web 20 × 80; ȳ = 67.8 mm from bottom, I = 3.14×10⁶ mm⁴), M = 2 kN·m sagging: top fibre (32.2 mm above NA) σ = 2×10⁶ × 32.2/3.14×10⁶ = 20.5 MPa compression; bottom (67.8 mm) 43.2 MPa tension.

**Example 3.** Rectangular beam turned on its side (d and b swapped, 100 × 200 → 200 × 100): Z halves ⇒ stress doubles for the same M.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using a single Z for unsymmetric sections.
- Orientation of rectangular beams (put the larger dimension vertical).
- Forgetting self-weight in design moments.

activity.prompt: Section → section modulus Z

quiz.q: Z_req for M = 30 kN·m, σ = 150 MPa
quiz.why: Z_req = M/σ_allow = 30×10⁶ N·mm/150 N/mm² = 2×10⁵ mm³. Convert kN·m to N·mm first.

quiz.q: Rotating a rectangle so d becomes the smaller side
quiz.why: Z = bd²/6 depends on the square of the depth in the plane of bending. If the larger side is turned to be the width, d falls and Z drops, so strength is reduced.

quiz.q: In an unsymmetric T-beam the larger stress occurs at
quiz.why: Bending stress is σ = My/I, so it is greatest at the fibre farthest from the neutral axis. In an unsymmetric section, this may be at the top or bottom.
options: the fibre farthest from the NA

quiz.q: Doubling beam depth (same b) multiplies Z by
quiz.why: Z = bd²/6, so doubling d multiplies Z by 2² = 4.

quiz.q: Stiffness of a beam is related to
quiz.why: The stiffness of a beam (resistance to deflection) depends on the flexural rigidity EI. It is the second moment of area I that sets the geometric part.

sources: Standard Strength of Materials syllabus (ME/CE core)

lessons.title: Shear stress in beams

scenes.text: Short, heavily loaded timber beams can split horizontally near the neutral axis.
That is where shear stress is greatest.

steps.title: Shear formula
steps.body:
τ = VAȳ/(Ib) (A ȳ = first moment of the area beyond the level about the NA; b = width at that level).
- Rectangle: parabolic, τ_max = 1.5τ_avg at the NA.
- Solid circle: τ_max = (4/3)τ_avg.
- I-section: most shear carried by the web; jump at the flange–web junction (width change); τ_max at the NA in the web.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** Rectangle 100 × 200, V = 40 kN: τ_avg = 2 MPa ⇒ τ_max = 3 MPa.

**Example 2.** Solid circle d = 100, V = 50 kN: τ_avg = 6.37 MPa ⇒ τ_max = 8.49 MPa.

**Example 3.** I-section approximation: τ_web ≈ V/(d × t_w): V = 100 kN, d = 300 mm, t_w = 8 mm ⇒ 41.7 MPa.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using total area for Aȳ (it's the area beyond the level only).
- Forgetting b changes at the flange–web junction.
- Assuming shear is maximum at the top fibre (it is zero there).

activity.prompt: Rectangular beam 120 × 250 mm with V = 60 kN. Maximum shear stress (MPa)?

quiz.why: The shear stress at a level of a beam is τ = VAȳ/(Ib), where A ȳ is the first moment of the area beyond that level and b is the width there.
For a rectangular section the shear stress is parabolic, τ_max = 3V/(2bd) at the neutral axis. Since τ_avg = V/(bd), the ratio is 1.5.
For a solid circular section, the maximum shear stress at the neutral axis is 4/3 of the average: τ_max = (4/3)τ_avg.
At the extreme fibres, the area beyond that level is zero, so Aȳ = 0 and the shear stress is zero.

quiz.q: In an I-beam, shear is carried mainly by
quiz.why: In an I-beam, the flanges carry most of the bending moment while the web, being narrow, carries most of the shear force.

sources: Standard Strength of Materials syllabus (ME/CE core)

lessons.title: Torsion of circular shafts

scenes.text: A drive shaft transmits engine torque to the wheels.
Hollow shafts carry nearly the same torque with much less weight.

steps.title: Torsion formula
steps.body:
T/J = τ/r = Gθ/L. J = πd⁴/32 (solid), π(D⁴ − d⁴)/32 (hollow). τ_max = 16T/(πd³) (solid).
Power P = 2πNT/60 (N in rpm, T in N·m, P in W).
Torsional stiffness k = GJ/L. Hollow shafts: for the same weight, stronger and stiffer than solid ones.
Combined bending and torsion: equivalent T_e = √(M² + T²) (max shear theory); M_e = ½(M + √(M² + T²)) (max normal stress).

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** Shaft transmits 100 kW at 300 rpm: T = 100 000 × 60/(2π × 300) = 3183 N·m. For τ = 60 MPa: d = ∛(16T/(πτ)) = ∛(16 × 3.183×10⁶/(π × 60)) = 64.6 mm ⇒ choose 65 mm.

**Example 2.** Hollow shaft D = 80, d = 60 mm under the same T: J = π(80⁴ − 60⁴)/32 = 2.749×10⁶ mm⁴; τ = 3.183×10⁶ × 40/2.749×10⁶ = 46.3 MPa.

**Example 3.** Twist of the solid 65 mm shaft over 2 m, G = 80 GPa: J = 1.752×10⁶; θ = TL/(GJ) = 3.183×10⁶ × 2000/(80 000 × 1.752×10⁶) = 0.0454 rad = 2.6°.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using rpm directly as ω (convert: ω = 2πN/60).
- Diameter vs radius in J.
- Forgetting the angle must be in radians in Gθ/L.

activity.prompt: Shaft transmits 15 kW at 1440 rpm. Torque (N·m, 1 decimal)?

quiz.why: The torsion formula for a circular shaft is T/J = τ/r = Gθ/L, linking torque, shear stress and angle of twist.
The polar second moment of area of a solid circular shaft is J = πd⁴/32, twice the I = πd⁴/64 about a diameter.
Power = torque × angular speed = T × 2πN/60, with N in rpm and T in N·m, giving watts.

quiz.q: Hollow vs solid shaft of equal weight
quiz.why: For the same weight (area), a hollow shaft has material further from the centre, so it has a larger J and transmits more torque for the same maximum shear stress.

For a shaft under bending M and torque T, the maximum shear stress theory uses the equivalent torque T_e = √(M² + T²), then sizes the shaft as if under pure torsion. The equivalent bending moment is ½(M + √(M² + T²)).

sources: Standard Strength of Materials syllabus (ME/CE core)

questions.q: Neutral axis passes through
questions.why: In pure bending, the neutral axis passes through the centroid of the cross-section, because the net axial force must be zero (tension equals compression).

questions.q: τ at the centre of a solid shaft in torsion
questions.why: In torsion, shear stress is τ = Tr/J, proportional to the radius. At the centre r = 0, so τ = 0, and the maximum is at the outer surface.

questions.q: Unit of section modulus
questions.why: Section modulus Z = I/y_max. I is in length⁴ and y in length, so Z is in length³, e.g. mm³.

questions.q: σ_max for M = 10 kN·m, Z = 10⁵ mm³
questions.why: σ_max = M/Z = 10×10⁶ N·mm/10⁵ mm³ = 100 MPa. Convert kN·m to N·mm first.

questions.q: τ_max for solid shaft d = 50, T = 1 kN·m
Shear avg 2 MPa in rectangle ⇒ max
questions.why: For a rectangular section, τ_max = 1.5 × τ_avg = 1.5 × 2 = 3 MPa, at the neutral axis.

questions.q: Assertion (A): Hollow shafts are preferred in aircraft and automobiles.  Reason (R): They give higher strength- and stiffness-to-weight ratios.
options: Both A and R are true, and R correctly explains A
Both A and R are true, but R does not explain A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
questions.why: Both are true. For the same weight, a hollow shaft puts material farther from the axis, where it resists torque best, so strength and stiffness per kilogram are higher. That is why it suits aircraft and cars.

questions.q: Z of hollow shaft D = 100, d = 80 mm
questions.why: For a hollow circular section, bending Z = I/(D/2) = π(D⁴ − d⁴)/(32D) = π(10⁸ − 4.096×10⁷)/(32 × 100) ≈ 57 962 mm³. The inner void removes some material, so Z is lower than that of the solid shaft (98 175 mm³).

questions.why: From τ = 16T/(πd³): d³ = 16 × 2×10⁶/(π × 80) = 127 324, so d = ∛127 324 ≈ 50.3 mm. Use N·mm and MPa consistently.

Case: A 4 m simply supported timber beam 150 × 300 mm carries a central 30 kN load. Max bending stress

lessons.title: Deflection of beams

scenes.text: A long bookshelf sags in the middle even if it doesn't break.
Deflection limits (e.g. span/250) often govern design more than strength.

steps.title: Method
steps.body:
EI d²y/dx² = M (double integration with boundary conditions). Macaulay's method handles discontinuous loads with ⟨x − a⟩ brackets (zero when negative).
Standard maximum deflections:
- Cantilever, end load W: WL³/(3EI), slope WL²/(2EI)
- Cantilever, UDL w: wL⁴/(8EI)
- Simply supported, central W: WL³/(48EI)
- Simply supported, UDL: 5wL⁴/(384EI)

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** Steel cantilever 2 m, W = 5 kN, I = 8×10⁶ mm⁴, E = 200 GPa: δ = 5000 × 2000³/(3 × 200 000 × 8×10⁶) = 8.33 mm.

**Example 2.** Simply supported 6 m, UDL 10 kN/m (= 10 N/mm), I = 10⁸ mm⁴: δ = 5 × 10 × 6000⁴/(384 × 200 000 × 10⁸) = 8.44 mm (span/711 ✔).

**Example 3.** Doubling span (UDL beam) multiplies deflection by 16.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Units: keep N and mm (w in N/mm).
- Forgetting boundary conditions (cantilever: y = 0 and slope = 0 at fixed end).
- Using WL³/48EI for an off-centre load.

activity.prompt: Simply supported 4 m beam, central load 20 kN, E = 200 GPa, I = 4×10⁷ mm⁴. Max deflection (mm, 2 decimals)?

quiz.why: The tip deflection of a cantilever with an end load W is δ = WL³/(3EI). The WL³/(48EI) is the central deflection of a simply supported beam.
The maximum deflection of a simply supported beam under a full UDL is 5wL⁴/(384EI), at mid-span.
For a UDL, deflection ∝ wL⁴/EI, so it varies as the fourth power of the span. Doubling L gives 16 times the deflection.

quiz.q: Macaulay brackets ⟨x − a⟩ are zero when
quiz.why: In Macaulay's method, the bracket ⟨x − a⟩ is included only after the point x passes a. For x < a it is zero.
Flexural rigidity is EI, the product of Young's modulus and second moment of area. It measures a beam's resistance to bending. GJ is torsional rigidity, EA axial.

lessons.title: Columns and buckling

scenes.text: Press down on a thin plastic ruler and it bows sideways long before it crushes.
Slender columns fail by buckling at Euler's critical load.

steps.title: Euler's formula
steps.body:
P_cr = π²EI/L_e². Effective length L_e: both ends pinned L; one fixed one free 2L; both fixed L/2; one fixed one pinned L/√2 (≈ 0.7L).
Slenderness ratio λ = L_e/k (k = √(I/A), use minimum I). Euler stress σ_cr = π²E/λ². Valid only for long columns (σ_cr below the proportional limit — steel λ > ~90–100).
**Rankine's formula** (all columns): P = σ_cA/(1 + a(L_e/k)²), a = σ_c/(π²E) (steel ≈ 1/7500).

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** Steel tube I = 1.2×10⁶ mm⁴, L = 3 m pinned–pinned, E = 200 GPa: P_cr = π² × 200 000 × 1.2×10⁶/3000² = 263 kN.

**Example 2.** Same column fixed–free: L_e = 6 m ⇒ P_cr = 65.8 kN (¼). Fixed–fixed: L_e = 1.5 m ⇒ 1053 kN (×4).

**Example 3.** Rankine: A = 2000 mm², k = 24.5 mm, L_e = 3000 mm, σ_c = 320 MPa, a = 1/7500: λ = 122.4; P = 320 × 2000/(1 + 14 989/7500) = 640 000/2.998 = 213 kN.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using maximum I instead of minimum I.
- Applying Euler to short columns (they crush first).
- Wrong effective length factor.

activity.prompt: Effective length L_e

quiz.why: Euler's critical load is P_cr = π²EI/L_e², where L_e is the effective length set by the end conditions.
A fixed–free column (like a flagpole) buckles with half a sine wave, so its effective length is 2L.
Euler's formula assumes elastic buckling and holds for slender columns. For short columns the stress reaches crushing before buckling, so it fails (overestimates the load).

quiz.q: Buckling occurs about the axis with
quiz.why: A column buckles about the axis with the smallest second moment of area, since that is the direction in which it is least stiff.
Fixed–fixed ends have L_e = L/2, and P_cr ∝ 1/L_e², so the load is 1/(0.5)² = 4 times that of a pinned–pinned column.

lessons.title: Principal stresses and Mohr's circle

story.title: Cracks at 45° in a twisted chalk

scenes.text: Twist a piece of chalk — it breaks along a 45° helix.
Mohr's circle shows the maximum tensile stress acts at 45° under pure shear.

steps.title: Plane stress
steps.body:
σ_n = (σₓ + σ_y)/2 + (σₓ − σ_y)/2 cos 2θ + τₓᵧ sin 2θ.
Principal stresses σ₁,₂ = (σₓ + σ_y)/2 ± √[((σₓ − σ_y)/2)² + τₓᵧ²]; principal planes tan 2θ_p = 2τₓᵧ/(σₓ − σ_y); no shear on them.
Max in-plane shear τ_max = (σ₁ − σ₂)/2 on planes at 45° to principal planes.
**Mohr's circle:** centre ((σₓ + σ_y)/2, 0), radius R = √[((σₓ − σ_y)/2)² + τ²]; angle 2θ on the circle = θ on the element.

steps.title: Theories of failure (basics)
steps.body: Max principal stress (Rankine) — brittle materials. Max shear stress (Tresca): σ₁ − σ₃ = σ_y. Max distortion energy (von Mises): √(σ₁² − σ₁σ₂ + σ₂²) = σ_y (plane stress) — ductile materials, most accurate.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** σₓ = 80, σ_y = 20, τ = 40 MPa: centre 50, R = √(900 + 1600) = 50 ⇒ σ₁ = 100, σ₂ = 0 MPa; τ_max = 50 MPa; 2θ_p = tan⁻¹(80/60) = 53.1° ⇒ θ_p = 26.6°.

**Example 2.** Pure shear τ = 60 MPa: σ₁ = 60, σ₂ = −60 at 45°.

**Example 3.** von Mises for σ₁ = 100, σ₂ = 0: σ_vm = 100 MPa.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using θ instead of 2θ on Mohr's circle.
- Sign convention for shear.
- Forgetting the third principal stress (0) when finding absolute max shear.

activity.prompt: σx = 60, σy = −20, τxy = 30 MPa. Major principal stress σ₁ (MPa)?

quiz.why: By definition, principal planes are planes with no shear stress. Only normal stresses (the principal stresses) act on them.
The centre of Mohr's circle lies on the normal-stress axis at the average normal stress, ((σ_x + σ_y)/2, 0), and the radius is the maximum shear stress.
The planes of maximum shear are at 45° to the principal planes, since on Mohr's circle they are 90° apart, i.e. half that in real space.
For ductile materials, the von Mises (distortion energy) theory agrees best with experiment. Max principal stress theory suits brittle materials.

quiz.q: Pure shear τ gives principal stresses
quiz.why: In pure shear τ, Mohr's circle is centred at the origin with radius τ. The principal stresses are +τ and −τ, at 45° to the shear planes.

lessons.title: Thin cylinders and spheres

scenes.text: LPG cylinders are thin steel shells under internal pressure.
The hoop stress is twice the longitudinal stress — so they split lengthwise.

steps.title: Formulas (t ≪ d, t < d/20)
steps.body:
Hoop (circumferential) σ_h = pd/(2t); longitudinal σ_l = pd/(4t) = σ_h/2. Sphere: σ = pd/(4t) (all directions).
With joint efficiency η: σ_h = pd/(2tη_l), σ_l = pd/(4tη_c).
Volumetric strain (cylinder): e_v = (pd/(4tE))(5 − 4ν); ΔV = e_v V. Sphere: e_v = (3pd/(4tE))(1 − ν).
Max shear (3-D, ignoring radial) = σ_h/2.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** Boiler d = 1.5 m, p = 1.2 MPa, σ_allow = 100 MPa: t = pd/(2σ) = 1.2 × 1500/200 = 9 mm (longitudinal stress 45 MPa).

**Example 2.** Cylinder d = 800 mm, t = 10 mm, p = 2 MPa: σ_h = 80 MPa, σ_l = 40 MPa.

**Example 3.** Sphere d = 1 m, t = 8 mm, p = 1.6 MPa: σ = 1.6 × 1000/32 = 50 MPa.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Swapping hoop and longitudinal formulas.
- Using radius in pd/(2t) (it uses diameter; with radius, σ_h = pr/t).
- Applying thin-shell formulas to thick cylinders (use Lamé).

activity.prompt: Thin cylinder d = 1000 mm, t = 10 mm, p = 1.5 MPa. Hoop stress (MPa)?

quiz.why: For a thin cylinder, a force balance on half the cylinder gives hoop stress σ_h = pd/(2t).
The longitudinal stress comes from pressure on the end area: pπd²/4 = σ_l × πdt, so σ_l = pd/(4t), half the hoop stress.

quiz.q: Thin cylinders tend to burst along
quiz.why: The hoop stress is twice the longitudinal stress, so a thin cylinder tends to split along a longitudinal line, where the hoop stress acts across.
options: a longitudinal line (due to hoop stress)

quiz.q: Sphere stress compared with cylinder hoop stress (same p, d, t)
quiz.why: A thin sphere has stress pd/(4t) in every direction, which is half the hoop stress pd/(2t) of a cylinder of the same size.
A cylinder is treated as thin-walled when t < d/20 (about 1/20 of the diameter), so the stress is nearly uniform through the thickness.

questions.why: Hoop stress pd/(2t) is twice the longitudinal stress pd/(4t).

questions.why: For equal biaxial stress and zero shear, Mohr's circle is a point: both principal stresses are 50 MPa, so σ₁ = 50 MPa.

questions.why: From σ_h = pd/(2t): t = pd/(2σ) = 1 × 2000/(2 × 100) = 10 mm. Use d in mm and stress in MPa.

options: Both A and R are true, and R correctly explains A
Both A and R are true, but R does not explain A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true

σₓ = 100, σ_y = 0, τ = 0: max shear
questions.why: With σ_x = 100 and the others zero, σ₁ = 100 and σ₂ = 0. τ_max = (σ₁ − σ₂)/2 = 50 MPa.

questions.q: τ_max for σₓ = 80, σ_y = −40, τ = 0
questions.why: The principal stresses are 80 and −40, so τ_max = (80 − (−40))/2 = 60 MPa. Subtract the signed values.

questions.q: Case: A 2.5 m steel strut (pinned) of solid round 40 mm. P_cr (E 200 GPa)
questions.why: I = π d⁴/64 = π × 40⁴/64 ≈ 125 664 mm⁴. P_cr = π²EI/L² = π² × 200 000 × 125 664/2500² ≈ 39 700 N = 39.7 kN, for pinned ends (L_e = L).

questions.q: Same strut: slenderness ratio
questions.why: k = √(I/A) = d/4 = 10 mm for a solid circle. Slenderness = L_e/k = 2500/10 = 250, so it is a very slender strut.

questions.q: Volumetric strain of thin cylinder (pd/(4tE))(5 − 4ν): p 2, d 1000, t 10, E 200 000, ν 0.3
Principal angle θ_p for σₓ = 60, σ_y = 0, τ = 30

questions.why: von Mises σ = √(σ₁² − σ₁σ₂ + σ₂²) = √(10 000 + 10 000 + 10 000) = √30 000 ≈ 173 MPa. For pure shear of 100 MPa it is √3 × 100.

steps.title: Patterns and allowances
steps.body:
Pattern materials: wood, metal, plastic, wax (investment). Types: solid, split, match-plate, cope-and-drag, loose-piece, sweep, skeleton.
Allowances: **shrinkage** (e.g. cast iron ~1%, steel ~2%, aluminium ~1.3%), **draft** (taper for withdrawal, 1–3°), **machining** (finish), **distortion** (camber), **shake** (negative — mould enlarges when rapped).

steps.title: Moulding sand
steps.body: Silica sand + clay binder (bentonite) + water (green sand) + additives (coal dust, cereal). Properties: permeability (lets gases escape), refractoriness, green and dry strength, cohesiveness, adhesiveness, collapsibility, flowability. AFS grain fineness number characterises grain size. Cores (oil/CO₂-bonded sand) form internal cavities; supported by core prints and chaplets.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** Steel casting 500 mm long, shrinkage 2%: pattern = 510 mm (before machining/draft).

**Example 2.** A 200 mm deep pocket with 2° draft: wall offset = 200 tan 2° = 7.0 mm.

**Example 3.** Low permeability sand ⇒ gas trapped ⇒ blowholes.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Adding shake allowance (it is negative).
- Forgetting cores need venting.
- Using too much water (lower strength, steam defects).

activity.prompt: Aluminium casting 400 mm, shrinkage 1.3%. Pattern length (mm, 1 decimal)?

quiz.why: Draft allowance is a slight taper on vertical faces of the pattern, so it can be withdrawn from the sand mould without breaking the mould edges.
Shake allowance is a negative allowance: the pattern is rapped to loosen it, which enlarges the mould cavity, so the pattern is made slightly smaller.
Permeability is the ability of the mould sand to let gases escape. Without it, trapped gas causes blowholes in the casting.
Chaplets are metal supports that hold cores in place in the mould cavity, and they melt into the casting.
Green sand is mainly silica sand with bentonite clay as the binder, plus water, for sand moulds.

scenes.text: Molten metal must fill the mould fast enough not to freeze, but smoothly enough not to erode sand.
Gating design uses Bernoulli and continuity.

steps.title: Elements and equations
steps.body:
Pouring basin → sprue → sprue well → runner → ingates. Sprue tapers to avoid aspiration: A₁/A₂ = √(h₂/h₁).
Velocity at sprue base V = √(2gh) (with C_d for losses). Pouring time t = V_cavity/(A_choke × V) (top gating). Bottom gating: t = (A_m/A_g)(√(2/g))(√h_t − √(h_t − h_m)).
Gating ratio (sprue : runner : ingate) e.g. 1:2:2 (unpressurised, less turbulence — aluminium) or 1:0.75:0.5 (pressurised — iron). Choke = smallest area controlling flow.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** Sprue height 200 mm: V = √(2 × 9.81 × 0.2) = 1.98 m/s.

**Example 2.** Cavity 0.002 m³, choke area 400 mm² (4×10⁻⁴ m²), V = 1.98 m/s: t = 0.002/(4×10⁻⁴ × 1.98) = 2.53 s.

**Example 3.** Sprue top area 600 mm² at h₁ = 50 mm (basin depth), bottom at h₂ = 250 mm: A₂ = 600√(50/250) = 268 mm².

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Straight (untapered) sprues cause air aspiration.
- Ignoring the choke location when computing time.
- Very high velocities causing sand erosion and inclusions.

activity.prompt: Sprue height 0.3 m. Ideal velocity at sprue base (m/s, 2 decimals)?

quiz.why: A tapered sprue keeps the liquid metal in contact with its walls as the velocity rises downward. This prevents low pressure, which would aspirate (suck in) air.
The choke is the smallest cross-sectional area in the gating system. It controls the flow rate of the metal into the mould.
Unpressurised gating (with area increasing downstream) reduces turbulence and oxide formation, which suits metals like aluminium that form oxide films readily.
By Bernoulli, metal falling a height h reaches the base of the sprue at velocity v = √(2gh).
By continuity, volume = flow rate × time, so pouring time = cavity volume/(choke area × velocity).

scenes.text: A cast part shows a hollow shrinkage pipe at its thickest section.
A riser must freeze after the casting to feed it.

steps.title: Chvorinov's rule
steps.body:
Solidification time t = C(V/A)ⁿ, n ≈ 2 (V/A = modulus). Riser must solidify later than the casting: (V/A)_riser ≥ 1.2(V/A)_casting typically.
For a cylindrical riser with H = D (side + top cooling, base on casting): V = πD³/4 and cooling area A = πD² (side) + πD²/4 (top) = 1.25πD² ⇒ V/A = D/5 (if the bottom also cools: D/6).
Shrinkage stages: liquid, solidification, solid contraction (pattern allowance covers solid only). Directional solidification towards the riser; chills accelerate cooling; exothermic sleeves and insulating toppings slow risers.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** Cube 100 mm: V/A = 100/6 = 16.67 mm. Plate 200 × 200 × 20: V/A = 800 000/(2 × 40 000 + 4 × 4000) = 800 000/96 000 = 8.33 mm ⇒ the cube takes 4× longer (ratio²).

**Example 2.** C = 2 s/mm² for a steel: cube t = 2 × 16.67² = 556 s.

**Example 3.** Riser for the cube (sides + top exposed, H = D): need D/5 ≥ 1.2 × 16.67 = 20 ⇒ D ≥ 100 mm.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using V/A of riser equal to casting (it must be larger).
- Forgetting that the riser's contact face does not cool.
- Placing risers far from heavy sections.

activity.prompt: Chvorinov: C = 1.5 s/mm², V/A = 10 mm, n = 2. Solidification time (s)?

quiz.why: Chvorinov's rule says solidification time t = C(V/A)². It grows with the square of the volume-to-surface-area ratio (modulus).
A riser must solidify after the casting so it can keep feeding liquid metal to make up for shrinkage until the casting is solid.
Chills (metal inserts) take heat quickly, so local solidification is faster. They help produce directional solidification towards the riser.
For a cube, V/A = a³/(6a²) = a/6 = 60/6 = 10 mm.
Shrinkage allowance makes up for solid contraction after solidification. Liquid and solidification shrinkage are made up by risers.

lessons.title: Casting defects and special casting processes

scenes.text: Jet-engine turbine blades are made by investment casting with ceramic shells.
Process choice decides surface finish, accuracy and defects.

steps.title: Defects and causes
steps.body:
- **Blowholes/porosity:** trapped gas — low permeability, moisture, poor venting.
- **Shrinkage cavity:** inadequate feeding.
- **Cold shut / misrun:** metal too cold or slow pouring — streams fail to fuse / mould not filled.
- **Hot tears:** restraint during cooling — poor collapsibility.
- **Inclusions, scabs, swells, mismatch (shift), fins.**

steps.title: Special processes
steps.body:
- **Die casting** (pressure, metal dies; Al/Zn/Mg; high rate, thin walls, good finish).
- **Investment (lost-wax):** wax pattern + ceramic shell; complex, precise parts (blades, jewellery, implants).
- **Centrifugal:** pipes, liners — dense outer structure.
- **Shell moulding:** resin-bonded sand shells — good finish.
- **Continuous casting:** billets/slabs in steel plants.
- **Permanent mould (gravity die).**

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** Defect: rounded smooth cavities near the top surface ⇒ blowholes ⇒ improve venting and reduce moisture.

**Example 2.** Centrifugal casting speed: G-factor = ω²R/g; for R = 0.2 m and G = 60: ω = √(60 × 9.81/0.2) = 54.2 rad/s ≈ 518 rpm.

**Example 3.** High-volume aluminium gearbox housings ⇒ pressure die casting.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Confusing cold shut (fusion failure) with hot tear (cracking during cooling).
- Using die casting for high-melting steels (die life too short).
- Ignoring the cost of dies for small batches.

activity.prompt: Defect → likely cause

quiz.why: Lost-wax casting is investment casting. A wax pattern is coated with ceramic and then melted out, leaving a precise mould.
Pipes are commonly made by centrifugal casting. The mould is spun, and the centrifugal force pushes metal against the wall, giving dense walls with no core.
Die casting uses permanent metal dies and needs metals with low melting points, such as aluminium, zinc and magnesium alloys.
A misrun happens when the metal solidifies before the cavity is filled, due to poor fluidity or low pouring temperature.
The G-factor in centrifugal casting is the ratio of centrifugal acceleration to gravity: G = ω²R/g.

questions.q: Draft is provided on
questions.why: Draft is a taper given to the vertical faces of a pattern so it can be drawn from the mould without damaging it.

questions.q: Investment casting uses
questions.why: Investment (lost-wax) casting uses a wax pattern, which is melted out of the ceramic shell before pouring.

questions.q: Blowholes are caused by
questions.why: Blowholes are cavities caused by gas trapped in the casting, often from moisture, or poor venting of the mould.

questions.q: Pattern for 300 mm steel part (2% shrinkage)
questions.why: Pattern size = casting size × (1 + shrinkage) = 300 × 1.02 = 306 mm.

questions.q: V/A of a sphere of diameter 60 mm
questions.why: For a sphere, V/A = (πD³/6)/(πD²) = D/6 = 60/6 = 10 mm.

questions.q: Velocity at sprue base for h = 0.5 m
Assertion (A): A riser must have a higher modulus (V/A) than the casting section it feeds.  Reason (R): By Chvorinov's rule, higher modulus means longer solidification time.
options: Both A and R are true, and R correctly explains A
Both A and R are true, but R does not explain A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
questions.why: Both are true. By Chvorinov's rule, solidification time grows with the modulus V/A, so a riser with a higher modulus freezes later and can feed the casting. R explains A.

questions.q: Pouring time: cavity 0.003 m³, choke 500 mm², V = 2 m/s
Solidification time ratio of two cubes 50 mm and 100 mm
questions.why: t ∝ (V/A)² and for cubes V/A = a/6. The sizes ratio is 1:2, so the times are in ratio 1:4.

questions.q: Tapered sprue: top 400 mm² at 40 mm head, bottom at 160 mm head
questions.why: By continuity and Bernoulli, area ∝ 1/√h, so A_bottom = 400 × √(40/160) = 400 × 0.5 = 200 mm².

questions.q: Case: Steel castings show hot tears at junctions. Best remedy
questions.why: Hot tears form when the casting is restrained as it contracts at hot spots. Improving mould collapsibility and adding fillets (to avoid sharp junctions) relieves the restraint.
options: improve mould collapsibility and add fillets

questions.q: Riser (H = D, top+side cooling) to feed a section of modulus 12.5 mm with factor 1.2
questions.why: For a cylindrical riser with H = D cooling from top and side, V/A = D/5. For the riser modulus 1.2 × 12.5 = 15 mm, D = 5 × 15 = 75 mm.
