Chvorinov C = 2 s/mm²: plate 100 × 100 × 10 mm, t
Gating ratio 1:2:2 is
questions.why: A gating ratio of 1:2:2 (sprue:runner:ingate) has increasing total area, so the metal flows in with low velocity and without back pressure. That makes it unpressurised.

courses.title: Manufacturing · Unit 2 · Welding and joining processes
courses.summary: Classification of welding, arc welding (SMAW, GMAW/MIG, GTAW/TIG, SAW), arc characteristics and heat input, gas welding and flames, resistance welding (spot, seam), solid-state processes (friction, ultrasonic), welding defects and inspection, soldering and brazing, and safety.
outcomes: Compare arc, gas, resistance and solid-state welding
Compute heat input and resistance-welding heat
Identify weld defects and inspection methods
Distinguish welding, brazing and soldering
courses.note: topic order may differ by edition

scenes.text: Shipyards weld kilometres of steel plate with submerged-arc and MIG processes.
An electric arc at about 5000+ °C melts the joint.

steps.title: Processes
steps.body:
- **SMAW (stick):** flux-coated consumable electrode; versatile, field work.
- **GMAW/MIG (and MAG):** continuous wire, shielding gas (Ar/CO₂); fast, semi-automatic.
- **GTAW/TIG:** non-consumable tungsten electrode, inert gas, filler optional; high quality, thin sheets, Al/stainless.
- **SAW:** arc under granular flux; thick plates, high deposition, flat position.
- **Plasma arc, electroslag** for special cases.
DCEN (straight polarity) — more heat in the workpiece (deeper penetration, TIG on steel); DCEP (reverse) — cleaning action (Al with AC/DCEP), more heat at the electrode.

steps.title: Heat input
steps.body: Heat input per unit length H = ηVI/v (η = arc efficiency: SAW ~0.9–0.99, SMAW/MIG ~0.7–0.85, TIG ~0.6–0.75). Higher heat input ⇒ wider heat-affected zone (HAZ), slower cooling.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** SMAW at 25 V, 200 A, 5 mm/s, η = 0.8: H = 0.8 × 25 × 200/5 = 800 J/mm.

**Example 2.** Doubling travel speed halves heat input (400 J/mm) — narrower HAZ.

**Example 3.** About 10 J/mm³ is needed to melt steel; with 50% melting efficiency the weld bead cross-section ≈ 800 × 0.5/10 = 40 mm².

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using a consumable-electrode process name for TIG.
- Ignoring arc efficiency in heat input.
- Welding without shielding/PPE — UV burns ('arc eye'), fumes: always use a helmet with the right filter shade and ventilation.

activity.prompt: Arc: V = 20 V, I = 150 A, travel 4 mm/s, η = 0.75. Heat input (J/mm)?

quiz.why: TIG (GTAW) uses a non-consumable tungsten electrode with an inert gas shield. Filler is added separately.

quiz.q: Process with arc hidden under flux
quiz.why: In submerged arc welding (SAW), the arc burns under a blanket of granular flux, so it is not visible.
DC electrode negative (DCEN, straight polarity) puts more heat on the workpiece, giving deeper penetration. DCEP heats the electrode more.
Heat input per unit length = ηVI/v, where v is the travel speed. It controls the size of the weld pool and HAZ.
AC TIG for aluminium gives a cleaning action during the positive half-cycle (which removes the oxide film) and penetration in the negative half-cycle.

scenes.text: A car body has thousands of spot welds made by robots in seconds.
Heat comes from the current flowing through the contact resistance.

steps.title: Gas welding (oxy-acetylene)
steps.body: C₂H₂ + O₂; flame ~3200 °C at the inner cone. Flames: **neutral** (1:1, most metals), **oxidising** (excess O₂ — brass, bronze), **carburising/reducing** (excess C₂H₂ — high-carbon steel, hard-facing). Also oxy-fuel cutting of steel.

steps.title: Resistance welding
steps.body: Heat H = I²Rt (Joule). Spot, seam (rollers — leak-tight joints), projection, flash and butt welding. Short times (0.1–0.5 s), very high currents (5–20 kA), low voltage. Electrodes: copper alloys (high conductivity, water-cooled).

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** Spot weld: I = 10 kA, R = 100 µΩ, t = 0.2 s: H = 10⁸ × 10⁻⁴ × 0.2 = 2000 J.

**Example 2.** If only 60% of that goes into the nugget and steel needs ≈ 10 J/mm³ to melt: nugget volume ≈ 120 mm³.

**Example 3.** Neutral flame for mild steel; oxidising for brass (prevents zinc fuming).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using a carburising flame on mild steel (adds carbon, brittle).
- Thinking resistance welding needs filler metal (it doesn't).
- Acetylene safety: never use above ~1 bar (15 psi) — explosive; use flashback arrestors.

activity.prompt: Flame type

quiz.why: Heat in resistance welding is by Joule heating, Q = I²Rt, using the resistance at the joint.
Seam welding is a continuous form of resistance welding using rotating roller electrodes, to make leak-tight seams.
The oxy-acetylene flame reaches about 3200 °C at the tip of the inner cone, the hottest of the common gas flames.
Spot welding electrodes are copper alloys, since they have high electrical and thermal conductivity, and they are water-cooled to avoid melting.

quiz.q: Spot weld heat: 8 kA, 150 µΩ, 0.25 s

scenes.text: Battery packs join aluminium and copper tabs — hard by fusion welding.
Ultrasonic and friction welding join them without melting.

steps.title: Solid-state processes
steps.body: Friction welding (rotary, linear), **friction stir welding** (non-consumable rotating tool; Al ship decks, aircraft panels), ultrasonic (thin foils, wires), explosive (cladding), diffusion bonding, forge welding. No melting ⇒ fewer solidification defects, dissimilar metals possible.

steps.title: Defects and inspection
steps.body:
Defects: porosity, slag inclusion, incomplete fusion, incomplete penetration, undercut, overlap, cracks (hot/cold/hydrogen), distortion, residual stresses.
Remedies: clean joints, dry electrodes (low-hydrogen), correct current/speed, preheat for high-carbon steels, post-weld heat treatment.
Inspection (NDT): visual, dye penetrant (surface cracks), magnetic particle (ferromagnetic, near-surface), ultrasonic (internal), radiography (X/γ — internal volumetric defects), eddy current.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** Cracks found hours after welding high-strength steel ⇒ hydrogen-induced cold cracking ⇒ use low-hydrogen electrodes, preheat.

**Example 2.** Aluminium aircraft panels ⇒ friction stir welding (no melting, low distortion).

**Example 3.** Internal porosity check in a pressure vessel weld ⇒ radiography or ultrasonic testing.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using magnetic particle testing on aluminium (non-ferromagnetic).
- Skipping preheat on high-carbon/alloy steels.
- Confusing undercut (groove at toe) with lack of penetration (root).

activity.prompt: NDT method → best for

quiz.q: Friction stir welding melts the metal?
quiz.why: Friction stir welding is a solid-state process. A rotating tool softens the metal by friction and stirs it, but the metal does not melt.
Hydrogen cracking needs hydrogen, a hard microstructure and stress. Low-hydrogen electrodes and preheating (slower cooling) lower these risks.
Magnetic particle testing works only on ferromagnetic materials, because it needs the part to be magnetised so a flaw disturbs the field and holds the particles.
Undercut is a groove melted into the base metal along the toe of a weld and not filled, which can act as a stress concentration.
options: a groove at the weld toe

quiz.why: Ultrasonic welding uses high-frequency vibration to join thin foils, wires and sheets, without much heat.

scenes.text: Electronics are joined by soldering at about 220 °C.
Plumbers braze copper pipes at much higher temperatures — the base metal never melts in either.

steps.title: Differences
steps.body:
- **Welding:** base metals melt (fusion) or bond in solid state.
- **Brazing:** filler melts above 450 °C (below base metal melting), flows by capillary action (brass, silver alloys); strong joints.
- **Soldering:** filler melts below 450 °C (Sn–Ag–Cu lead-free solders ~217–220 °C; traditional Sn–Pb ~183 °C); electronics.
Flux removes oxides and promotes wetting. Joint clearance small (0.025–0.15 mm) for capillary flow.
**Adhesive bonding:** epoxies, cyanoacrylates — dissimilar materials, distributes stress; limited temperature resistance.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** Copper water pipes ⇒ brazing (or soldering for low-temperature plumbing) with capillary fittings.

**Example 2.** Lap length for a brazed joint in shear to match the base strip strength: L = σ_t t/τ_filler; σ_t = 300 MPa, t = 2 mm, τ = 100 MPa ⇒ L = 6 mm.

**Example 3.** Lead-free solder required for consumer electronics in many markets (RoHS rules).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Calling brazing a welding process (base metal doesn't melt).
- Too large a joint gap (capillary action fails).
- Breathing flux fumes — ventilate and avoid lead exposure.

statements.s: In brazing, the base metal melts.
Flux removes oxides and helps wetting.

quiz.why: By definition, brazing uses a filler metal that melts above 450 °C but below the melting point of the base metals. Below 450 °C it is soldering.
Typical lead-free (tin–silver–copper) solders melt around 217–220 °C, which is higher than older tin–lead solders (about 183 °C).

quiz.q: Filler flows into the joint by
quiz.why: In brazing and soldering, molten filler is drawn into the narrow gap between close-fitting parts by capillary action, provided it wets the surfaces.

quiz.q: Lap length for σ 250 MPa, t 3 mm, τ 75 MPa
quiz.why: Equal strength of plate and joint: σ × t = τ × L, so L = σt/τ = 250 × 3/75 = 10 mm.
Adhesives are polymers, so they lose strength at higher temperatures. They can join dissimilar materials and spread the stress, so those are not limitations.

questions.q: Non-consumable electrode process
questions.why: TIG uses a non-consumable tungsten electrode. SAW, MIG and SMAW (stick) electrodes are consumed and become the filler metal.

questions.q: Spot welding is a type of
questions.why: Spot welding joins sheets by heat from electrical resistance at a point, so it is a form of resistance welding.

questions.q: Flame for mild steel
questions.why: A neutral flame (equal oxygen and acetylene) is used for mild steel, as it neither adds carbon nor oxidises the metal.

questions.q: Heat input: 30 V, 250 A, 6 mm/s, η 0.9
Spot weld: 12 kA, 80 µΩ, 0.3 s
Internal porosity best detected by
questions.why: Internal porosity is a volume defect. Radiography (X-ray or gamma) sees through the weld, while dye penetrant and visual only find surface defects.

questions.q: Assertion (A): Friction stir welding is suitable for aluminium alloys that are hard to fusion weld.  Reason (R): It joins metal in the solid state without melting, avoiding solidification cracking.
options: Both A and R are true, and R correctly explains A
Both A and R are true, but R does not explain A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
questions.why: Both are true. Many aluminium alloys crack when fusion welded as they solidify. Friction stir welding stays below the melting point, so there is no solidification cracking. R explains A.

questions.q: Halving current (same V, speed, η) changes heat input to
questions.why: Heat input is ηVI/v, linear in current. Halving I halves the heat input, with V, speed and efficiency constant.

questions.q: Cold cracking in high-strength steel is linked to
questions.why: Cold (hydrogen-induced) cracking occurs in the HAZ of high-strength steels when hydrogen, a hard microstructure and residual stress are present together.

questions.q: Brazed lap length: σ 400 MPa, t 1.5 mm, τ 120 MPa
questions.why: For equal strength, σt = τL, so L = 400 × 1.5/120 = 5 mm.

questions.q: Case: A fabricator must weld 40 mm thick steel plates in the flat position at high deposition rate. Best process
questions.why: Submerged arc welding gives very high deposition rates and deep penetration, which suits thick plates (40 mm) in the flat position. TIG is too slow, and soldering is too weak.

questions.q: Case: Welding thin (1 mm) stainless steel sheets for food equipment with best finish
questions.why: TIG gives precise, clean, low-spatter welds on thin stainless steel, which gives the best finish for food equipment.

questions.q: Energy to melt 50 mm³ of steel at 10 J/mm³ with 25% process efficiency (energy supplied)
questions.why: Energy needed in the metal = 50 × 10 = 500 J. At 25% efficiency, the energy supplied = 500/0.25 = 2000 J.

questions.q: Spot weld nugget heat needed 3000 J with R = 120 µΩ, t = 0.25 s: current
Magnetic particle inspection on austenitic stainless steel welds
questions.why: Austenitic stainless steel is non-magnetic, so magnetic particle inspection does not work. Dye penetrant or radiography is used instead.

courses.summary: Hot and cold working, recrystallisation, flow stress and true strain, rolling (draft, roll force, maximum draft), forging (open/closed die, forging force), extrusion and wire drawing (reduction, forces), and sheet-metal operations (shearing, blanking/punching force, clearance, bending, deep drawing).
outcomes: Distinguish hot and cold working using recrystallisation temperature
Compute true strain, draft and roll-force estimates
Estimate forging, extrusion and drawing loads
Compute blanking force, clearance and deep-drawing limits

lessons.title: Hot and cold working; true stress and strain

scenes.text: Bend a paper clip back and forth and it gets harder, then snaps.
That is strain hardening — hot working avoids it by recrystallising as it goes.

steps.title: Concepts
steps.body:
Recrystallisation temperature ≈ 0.4–0.5 T_m (K). **Hot working** above it (low forces, no strain hardening, poorer finish/tolerance, scale). **Cold working** below it (strain hardening, better finish and accuracy, higher forces, reduced ductility). Warm working in between.
True strain ε = ln(L/L₀) = ln(A₀/A); flow stress σ_f = Kεⁿ (n = strain-hardening exponent). Volume constancy in plastic deformation: A₀L₀ = AL.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** Lead (T_m ≈ 600 K): recrystallisation ≈ 240–300 K ⇒ room-temperature working of lead is hot working!

**Example 2.** Bar from 50 mm to 40 mm dia: ε = ln(2500/1600) = 0.446.

**Example 3.** K = 500 MPa, n = 0.2 at ε = 0.446: σ_f = 500 × 0.446^0.2 = 425 MPa.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using engineering strain for large deformations.
- Forgetting temperatures in kelvin for 0.4T_m.
- Assuming hot working gives better surface finish.

activity.prompt: True strain for reducing a rod area from 400 mm² to 200 mm² (3 decimals)?

quiz.why: Hot working is done above the recrystallisation temperature, so new strain-free grains form as the metal deforms and it does not strain-harden.
Cold working, below the recrystallisation temperature, raises the dislocation density and so the strength and hardness: strain hardening.
True strain is ε = ln(L/L₀), the sum of small increments dL/L. Engineering strain is (L − L₀)/L₀.
In plastic deformation, volume stays constant, as metals are essentially incompressible when yielding.
Cold working gives better dimensional accuracy and finish than hot working, because there is no scale and little thermal contraction.

scenes.text: A steel mill reduces a 200 mm slab to a 2 mm sheet through many roll passes.
Friction pulls the metal into the roll gap — up to a maximum draft.

steps.title: Rolling relations
steps.body:
Draft Δh = h₀ − h_f. Maximum draft Δh_max = μ²R (R = roll radius, μ = friction coefficient). Bite angle condition μ ≥ tan α.
Projected contact length L ≈ √(RΔh). Roll force (approx.) F = σ̄_f w L (σ̄_f = average flow stress). Torque per roll T = F L/2; power (two rolls) P = 2πNFL/60 (approx.).
Neutral point: roll and strip speeds equal; forward slip beyond it.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** R = 250 mm, μ = 0.12: Δh_max = 0.0144 × 250 = 3.6 mm.

**Example 2.** Strip 300 mm wide from 25 to 22 mm, R = 250 mm, σ̄_f = 180 MPa: L = √(250 × 3) = 27.4 mm; F = 180 × 300 × 27.4 = 1.48 MN.

**Example 3.** Torque per roll = 1.48×10⁶ × 0.0274/2 = 20.3 kN·m; at 50 rpm both rolls: P = 2 × 2π × 50 × 20.3×10³/60 = 213 kW.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using diameter instead of radius in μ²R.
- Forgetting both rolls in power.
- Too large a draft ⇒ the strip won't be drawn in (skidding).

activity.prompt: Maximum draft: μ = 0.1, roll radius 300 mm (mm)?

quiz.why: For rolling, the strip is drawn in if μ ≥ tanα, which gives the maximum draft Δh_max = μ²R.
The projected contact length in rolling is L = √(RΔh), from the geometry of the roll arc.
At the neutral point in rolling, the strip speed equals the roll surface speed. Before it the strip is slower, and after it the strip is faster.
options: strip and roll speeds are equal

quiz.why: Maximum draft is μ²R, so a larger roll radius allows a bigger reduction per pass. But it increases the contact length and so the roll force.
Hot rolling oxidises the surface, giving scale, and thermal contraction on cooling makes the dimensions less accurate than cold rolling.

scenes.text: Crankshafts are forged for strength; copper wires are drawn through dies.
Grain flow follows the shape in forging — tougher parts.

steps.title: Forging
steps.body:
Open-die (simple shapes, large parts), closed/impression-die (flash), upsetting, coining. Forged parts have continuous grain flow ⇒ better fatigue strength.
Forging force (cylinder, with friction): F = σ_f A (1 + 2μr/(3h)) (r = radius, h = height).

steps.title: Extrusion and drawing
steps.body:
Extrusion: direct (forward), indirect (backward), impact, hydrostatic. Extrusion ratio R = A₀/A_f; ideal pressure p = σ̄_f ln R (real higher due to friction: Johnson's p = σ̄_f(a + b ln R), a ≈ 0.8, b ≈ 1.2–1.5).
Wire drawing: stress σ_d = σ̄_f ln(A₀/A_f) (ideal); must be below σ_f of the drawn wire ⇒ max ideal reduction per pass: ln(A₀/A_f) = 1 ⇒ 63% reduction (practically ~30–45%).

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** Upsetting Ø50 × 50 mm to 25 mm height: final r = 35.36 mm; σ_f = 300 MPa, μ = 0.2: A = 3927 mm²; F = 300 × 3927 × (1 + 2 × 0.2 × 35.36/(3 × 25)) = 1.178 MN × 1.189 = 1.40 MN.

**Example 2.** Extrusion 100 → 50 mm dia: R = 4; ideal p = σ̄_f ln 4 = 1.386 σ̄_f; with σ̄_f = 150 MPa ⇒ 208 MPa.

**Example 3.** Wire 5 → 4 mm: ln(25/16) = 0.446 ⇒ σ_d = 0.446 σ̄_f — feasible.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using initial area for forging force at the end of the stroke.
- Ignoring friction and redundant work (ideal estimates are low).
- Excessive reduction per pass in drawing ⇒ wire breaks.

activity.prompt: Extrusion ratio 8, average flow stress 100 MPa. Ideal extrusion pressure (MPa, 1 decimal)?

quiz.q: Forged parts are strong due to
quiz.why: Forging gives a continuous grain flow that follows the part's shape, which adds strength and toughness, unlike casting or machining from bar.
The ideal extrusion pressure (no friction) is p = σ̄_f ln R, where R = A₀/A_f is the extrusion ratio.

quiz.q: Max ideal reduction in wire drawing per pass
quiz.why: In ideal wire drawing, σ_d = σ̄_f ln(A₀/A). With σ_d at most equal to σ̄_f, ln(A₀/A) ≤ 1, so A₀/A ≤ e, and the maximum reduction is 1 − 1/e ≈ 63%.
In indirect (backward) extrusion, the billet stays still relative to the container and the die moves. There is no relative sliding, so friction is lower.
options: container and billet move together; less friction

quiz.why: Flash forms in closed-die forging. Excess metal squeezes out between the die halves, and also helps fill the die cavity.

scenes.text: A press punches thousands of washers per hour from steel strip.
Blanking force and die clearance decide tool size and edge quality.

steps.title: Shearing
steps.body:
Blanking (keep the piece) vs punching/piercing (keep the strip). Force F = L t τ_s (L = cut perimeter, τ_s ≈ 0.7–0.8 UTS). Clearance per side c ≈ k t (k ≈ 0.03–0.1 depending on material).
Blanking: die = blank size, punch = die − 2c. Punching: punch = hole size, die = punch + 2c.
Shear on punch (angled) reduces peak force.

steps.title: Bending and deep drawing
steps.body:
Bending: minimum bend radius ∝ t (depends on ductility); springback (more for high strength, large R/t) — compensate by overbending. Bend allowance BA = α(R + kt) (α in radians, k ≈ 0.33–0.5).
Deep drawing: limiting drawing ratio LDR = D_blank/d_punch ≈ 2; blank diameter for a cup (no flange) D = √(d² + 4dh); blank holder prevents wrinkling; drawing force F ≈ πd t UTS (D/d − 0.7).

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** Washer: outer Ø40, hole Ø20, t = 2 mm, τ_s = 300 MPa. Blanking F = π × 40 × 2 × 300 = 75.4 kN; punching F = 37.7 kN.

**Example 2.** Clearance 5% of t = 0.1 mm per side: blanking die 40.00, punch 39.80 mm; piercing punch 20.00, die 20.20 mm.

**Example 3.** Cup d = 50, h = 40: D = √(2500 + 8000) = 102.5 mm ⇒ D/d = 2.05 ⇒ needs two draws (LDR ≈ 2).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Putting clearance on the wrong tool (die for blanking, punch side for piercing).
- Using UTS instead of shear strength.
- Ignoring springback in bending.

activity.prompt: Blank a 50 mm square (perimeter 200 mm) from 3 mm sheet, τ = 250 MPa. Force (kN)?

quiz.why: Blanking force F = L × t × τ_s, the cutting perimeter times the thickness times the shear strength, which is the shear area times τ.

quiz.q: In blanking, clearance is applied to
quiz.why: In blanking, the die opening is made to the blank size and the punch is smaller (clearance on the punch). In punching holes it is the other way round.
The limiting drawing ratio (blank diameter/punch diameter) for a single draw is typically about 2. Beyond it the cup tears.
Springback is the elastic recovery after bending. It is larger for high-yield-strength materials and for larger bend radius to thickness ratios.

quiz.q: Blank diameter of cup d 40, h 30
quiz.why: For a cup, equal surface area gives blank D = √(d² + 4dh) = √(1600 + 4 × 40 × 30) = √6400 = 80 mm.

questions.q: Recrystallisation temperature ≈
questions.why: The recrystallisation temperature is typically 0.4 to 0.5 of the absolute melting point T_m. Hot working is above it.

questions.q: Wire drawing is
questions.why: In wire drawing, the wire is pulled through a die, which reduces its diameter. The material has to be in tension, so pushing would buckle it.

questions.q: Blanking: useful part is
questions.why: In blanking, the piece punched out is the useful part, and the remaining strip is scrap. In piercing, the slug is the scrap.

questions.q: Max draft for μ 0.15, R 400 mm
True strain for L 100 → 150 mm
questions.why: True strain = ln(150/100) = ln 1.5 ≈ 0.405.

questions.q: Punching force: hole Ø25, t 4, τ 300 MPa
questions.why: F = π d t τ = π × 25 × 4 × 300 ≈ 94 200 N = 94.2 kN. It is the shear area (perimeter × thickness) times the shear strength.

questions.q: Assertion (A): Cold-worked parts have better surface finish than hot-worked parts.  Reason (R): No oxide scale forms at low temperatures.
options: Both A and R are true, and R correctly explains A
Both A and R are true, but R does not explain A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
questions.why: Both are true. At low temperatures, no oxide scale forms, so the surface stays smooth and bright. In hot working, scale roughens it. R explains A.

questions.q: Rolling contact length R 300, Δh 3 mm
questions.why: Contact length L = √(RΔh) = √(300 × 3) = √900 = 30 mm.

questions.q: Flow stress K 600, n 0.25 at ε = 0.5
Roll force: w 200 mm, L 20 mm, σ̄ 200 MPa
questions.why: Roll force = σ̄ × w × L = 200 × 200 × 20 = 800 000 N = 0.8 MN, using the projected contact area (w × L).

questions.q: Case: A 1.5 mm steel strip (τ 350 MPa) is blanked into Ø60 discs. Press capacity needed with 20% margin
questions.why: F = π d t τ = π × 60 × 1.5 × 350 ≈ 98.96 kN. With a 20% margin: 98.96 × 1.2 ≈ 119 kN of press capacity.

questions.q: Upsetting force: σ_f 250 MPa, final A 2000 mm², μ 0.1, r 25, h 20
questions.why: Ideal force = σ_f × A = 250 × 2000 = 0.5 MN. Friction raises it by the factor (1 + 2μr/(3h)) = 1 + 2 × 0.1 × 25/60 = 1.083, so F ≈ 0.542 MN.

questions.q: Number of draws for cup d 40, h 60 (LDR 2)
questions.why: The blank D = √(d² + 4dh) = √(1600 + 9600) = 105.8 mm. D/d = 2.65, which is more than the limiting ratio of 2, so two or more draws are needed.

questions.q: Ideal drawing stress ratio σ_d/σ̄_f for 6 → 5 mm wire
questions.why: Ideal drawing stress ratio = ln(A₀/A) = ln(6²/5²) = ln(1.44) ≈ 0.365. It must stay below 1.

questions.q: Punch diameter for piercing a Ø30 hole, clearance 0.15 mm per side
questions.why: When piercing a hole, the hole size is set by the punch, so the punch is 30.00 mm. The die is larger by the clearance on both sides: 30 + 2 × 0.15 = 30.30 mm.

scenes.text: A lathe peels long curly chips off a steel shaft.
Chip thickness reveals the shear angle and cutting forces.

steps.title: Relations
steps.body:
Chip thickness ratio r = t₁/t₂ (< 1). Shear angle tan φ = r cos α/(1 − r sin α) (α = rake angle).
Merchant's theory: 2φ + β − α = 90° (β = friction angle, μ = tan β).
Forces: F_c (cutting), F_t (thrust). Friction force F = F_c sin α + F_t cos α; normal N = F_c cos α − F_t sin α; μ = F/N.
Shear force F_s = F_c cos φ − F_t sin φ; shear stress τ = F_s/A_s with A_s = bt₁/sin φ.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Inverting the chip ratio (t₁/t₂, not t₂/t₁).
- Using degrees inconsistently in trig functions.
- Assuming Merchant's equation is exact (it's an idealisation).

activity.prompt: Chip ratio r = 0.5, rake α = 0°. Shear angle φ (degrees, 2 decimals)?

quiz.why: The chip thickness ratio r = t₁/t₂ (uncut thickness/chip thickness). Since the chip is thicker than the uncut layer, r is below 1.
Merchant's relation (minimum energy): 2φ + β − α = 90°, where φ is the shear angle, β the friction angle and α the rake angle.
A larger rake angle makes the cutting easier: the shear angle rises, the shear plane gets shorter, so the forces and power fall.

quiz.q: Friction coefficient on the tool face
quiz.why: The coefficient of friction on the tool face is μ = F/N, the ratio of the friction force to the normal force there.

quiz.q: Orthogonal cutting means the edge is
quiz.why: In orthogonal cutting, the cutting edge is perpendicular to the cutting velocity, giving a simple 2-D plane strain model.

lessons.title: Cutting power, tool materials and tool life

scenes.text: A shop switches from HSS tools to carbide inserts and quadruples cutting speed.
Taylor's equation predicts how long each tool lasts.

steps.title: Power and specific energy
steps.body: Cutting power P = F_c V. Material removal rate (turning) MRR = V f d (f feed, d depth of cut). Specific cutting energy u = P/MRR = F_c/(f d) (J/mm³ or N/mm²).

steps.title: Tool materials and Taylor
steps.body:
Increasing hot hardness: carbon steel < HSS < cast alloys < cemented carbide (coated) < cermets < ceramics < CBN < diamond (PCD — not for steel; reacts with iron).
**Taylor's equation:** VTⁿ = C (n ≈ 0.1 HSS, 0.2–0.3 carbide, 0.5–0.7 ceramics). Extended: VTⁿf^a d^b = C.
Tool wear: flank wear (VB criterion ~0.3 mm), crater wear, notch; chipping. Economics: minimum-cost tool life T = (1/n − 1)(C_t/C_m + t_c).

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** F_c = 1000 N, V = 120 m/min = 2 m/s: P = 2 kW. MRR at f = 0.25 mm, d = 2 mm: 2000 × 0.25 × 2 = 1000 mm³/s ⇒ u = 2 J/mm³.

**Example 2.** Carbide n = 0.25: tool life 60 min at 100 m/min ⇒ C = 100 × 60^0.25 = 278.3. At 150 m/min: T = (278.3/150)^4 = 11.9 min.

**Example 3.** Doubling speed with n = 0.125 (HSS): T falls by 2^8 = 256 times.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using m/min with N to get watts (convert to m/s).
- Using diamond tools on steel.
- Rearranging Taylor: T = (C/V)^(1/n).

activity.prompt: Taylor: n = 0.2, C = 300 (m/min, min). Tool life at V = 150 m/min (min)?

quiz.why: Taylor's tool life equation is VTⁿ = C, linking cutting speed V and tool life T.
Diamond reacts with iron (carbon diffuses into steel) at cutting temperatures, so it wears quickly. It is not used for steel, but for non-ferrous metals and ceramics.
Specific cutting energy is the energy per unit volume of metal removed: F_c/(f d), the cutting force over the chip cross-section.
The Taylor exponent n is about 0.1–0.15 for HSS, 0.2–0.3 for carbide and 0.4–0.6 for ceramics.
A common tool-life criterion is a flank wear VB of about 0.3 mm (ISO uses 0.3 mm for uniform wear).

scenes.text: A production planner estimates cycle times for turning, drilling and milling a part.
Simple formulas give machining time per operation.

steps.title: Time formulas
steps.body:
- **Turning:** N = 1000V/(πD) rpm; time per pass t = L/(fN) (L includes approach/overtravel).
- **Drilling:** t = (L + 0.3D)/(fN) (approach for the drill point ≈ 0.3D for 118°).
- **Milling (slab/face):** table feed f_m = f_z z N (mm/min); t = (L + approach)/f_m; MRR = w d f_m.
- **Grinding:** fine finish, abrasive wheels (Al₂O₃ for steel, SiC for cast iron/non-ferrous); dressing restores sharpness.
Surface roughness (turning, ideal) R_max = f²/(8r) (r = nose radius).

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** Turn Ø50 × 200 mm at V = 100 m/min, f = 0.2 mm/rev: N = 636.6 rpm; t = 200/(0.2 × 636.6) = 1.57 min per pass.

**Example 2.** Drill Ø20 × 40 mm, V = 25 m/min, f = 0.25: N = 398 rpm; t = (40 + 6)/(0.25 × 398) = 0.46 min.

**Example 3.** Face mill: 8 teeth, f_z = 0.1 mm, N = 500 rpm ⇒ f_m = 400 mm/min; 300 mm length + 100 approach ⇒ 1 min.

**Example 4.** R_max for f = 0.2 mm, r = 0.8 mm: 0.04/6.4 = 6.25 µm.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using radius in N = 1000V/(πD).
- Forgetting approach/overtravel.
- Units: f_z per tooth vs per revolution.

activity.prompt: Turning speed: V = 120 m/min on Ø40 mm. Spindle speed (rpm, nearest whole)?

quiz.why: Spindle speed N = 1000V/(πD) rpm, with V in m/min and D in mm.
Milling table feed = feed per tooth × number of teeth × spindle speed: f_z × z × N.
The ideal peak-to-valley roughness in turning is R_max = f²/(8r), where f is the feed and r the nose radius.
Silicon carbide wheels suit cast iron, and non-ferrous and non-metallic materials. Aluminium oxide is for steels.
A 118° drill point has a cone height of (D/2)/tan(59°) ≈ 0.3D, so the drill travels this extra distance before reaching full diameter.

story.title: Making a turbine blade cooling hole

scenes.text: Tiny angled cooling holes in superalloy blades are drilled by EDM or lasers.
Prototype brackets are 3-D printed overnight.

steps.title: Non-traditional processes
steps.body:
- **EDM:** sparks erode conductive workpieces (dies, hard materials); wire-EDM for profiles.
- **ECM:** anodic dissolution (no tool wear, stress-free).
- **USM:** abrasive slurry + vibrating tool (brittle materials: glass, ceramics).
- **AJM/WJM:** abrasive/water jets (cutting composites, stone).
- **LBM/EBM:** lasers/electron beams (micro-holes, cutting, welding).
- **Chemical machining (etching).**

steps.title: CNC and additive manufacturing
steps.body:
CNC: G-codes (G00 rapid, G01 linear feed, G02/G03 arcs, G90 absolute, G91 incremental), M-codes (M03 spindle on CW, M05 stop, M08 coolant, M30 end). CAD/CAM generates toolpaths; DNC/flexible manufacturing.
Additive manufacturing (ISO/ASTM 52900 categories): material extrusion (FDM/FFF), vat photopolymerisation (SLA/DLP), powder bed fusion (SLS, SLM/DMLS, EBM), material jetting, binder jetting, directed energy deposition, sheet lamination. Strengths: complex geometry, lattices, customisation; limits: speed, surface finish, anisotropy, post-processing.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** Hardened tool steel die cavity ⇒ EDM (sinker).

**Example 2.** Glass micro-holes ⇒ USM.

**Example 3.** CNC snippet: G90 G01 X50 Z−20 F0.2 — absolute linear move to (50, −20) at 0.2 mm/rev.

**Example 4.** Titanium patient-specific implant ⇒ powder bed fusion (SLM/EBM).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- EDM on non-conducting ceramics (won't work).
- Confusing G02 (clockwise) and G03 (counter-clockwise).
- Assuming 3-D printed parts are isotropic and production-ready without post-processing.

quiz.why: G01 is linear interpolation at the programmed feed rate. G00 is rapid positioning and G02/G03 are circular arcs.
M03 turns the spindle on in the clockwise direction. M05 stops it, and M30 ends the program.

quiz.q: EDM requires the workpiece to be
quiz.why: Electrical discharge machining removes metal with sparks between electrode and workpiece, so the workpiece must be electrically conductive.
FDM (fused deposition modelling) pushes melted thermoplastic filament through a nozzle, which is material extrusion in 3D-printing terms.
In electrochemical machining, the tool does not touch the work and is not worn away, so tool wear is practically zero.

quiz.why: The negative allowance in patterns is the shake allowance: rapping the pattern enlarges the cavity, so the pattern is made smaller.

quiz.q: Mock 1: Process with non-consumable tungsten electrode
quiz.why: TIG (GTAW) uses a non-consumable tungsten electrode with inert gas shielding.
Hot working takes place above the recrystallisation temperature of the metal.
True strain = ln(L/L₀) = ln(100/50) = ln 2 ≈ 0.693.

questions.q: Sand property letting gases escape
questions.why: Permeability is the ability of the moulding sand to let gases escape. Cohesiveness is about holding together, refractoriness about heat resistance, and collapsibility about yielding to casting shrinkage.

questions.q: Soldering temperature limit
questions.why: Soldering uses a filler that melts below 450 °C. Brazing uses one that melts above 450 °C but below the base metal's melting point.

questions.q: Extrusion pushes metal
questions.why: In extrusion, a billet is pushed (or pulled) through a die opening to give a long constant-section product.

questions.q: Fastest-wearing tool when V doubles (n smallest)
questions.why: Tool life varies as T ∝ V^(−1/n). The smaller the n, the more strongly life falls when speed rises, so HSS (n about 0.1–0.15) suffers the most.

questions.q: Pattern for 250 mm cast iron (1% shrinkage)
questions.why: Pattern size = 250 × 1.01 = 252.5 mm. The pattern is made bigger to allow for the shrinkage of the casting.

questions.q: Pouring time: 0.0015 m³ cavity, choke 300 mm², V 2.5 m/s
Heat input 25 V, 180 A, 4.5 mm/s, η 0.8
Cup blank: d 60, h 45
Assertion (A): Closed-die forging produces flash.  Reason (R): Excess metal escapes into the flash gutter to ensure complete die filling.
options: Both A and R are true, and R correctly explains A
Both A and R are true, but R does not explain A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
questions.why: Both are true. In closed-die forging, extra metal is deliberately supplied. It squeezes out as flash, which makes sure that the die fills fully. R explains A.

questions.q: Roll force: w 250, Δh 4, R 400, σ̄ 160 MPa
questions.why: Contact length L = √(RΔh) = √(400 × 4) = 40 mm. Force = σ̄ w L = 160 × 250 × 40 = 1.6×10⁶ N = 1.6 MN.

questions.q: Shear angle r 0.4, α 0°
questions.why: For α = 0, tanφ = r = 0.4, so φ = tan⁻¹(0.4) ≈ 21.8°.

questions.q: Chvorinov C 3 s/mm², cylinder D 60 (all faces cooling, H = D): t
questions.why: For a cylinder with H = D, V/A = (πD³/4)/(1.5πD²) = D/6 = 10 mm. t = C(V/A)² = 3 × 100 = 300 s.

questions.q: Taylor: tool life 30 min at 100 m/min (n 0.25). Life at 80 m/min
questions.why: Taylor's equation gives T ∝ V^(−1/n) = V⁻⁴. At a lower speed, T₂ = 30 × (100/80)⁴ = 30 × 2.44 ≈ 73 min. A 20% speed cut gives more than double the tool life.

questions.q: Case: A 2 mm steel washer (OD 50, ID 25, τ 320 MPa) is made in a single stroke compound die (blank + pierce together). Total force
questions.why: A compound die cuts both the outer blank and the inner hole in one stroke, so the force adds up the two cut perimeters: π(50 + 25) × 2 × 320 = π × 75 × 2 × 320 ≈ 150.8 kN.

questions.q: Specific energy 3 J/mm³, MRR 800 mm³/s: power
questions.why: Power = specific energy × material removal rate = 3 J/mm³ × 800 mm³/s = 2400 W = 2.4 kW.

questions.q: Extrusion Johnson: σ̄ 120 MPa, R 10, a 0.8, b 1.5
questions.why: Johnson's extrusion formula is p = σ̄(a + b ln R). With R = 10, ln R = 2.303, so p = 120 × (0.8 + 1.5 × 2.303) = 120 × 4.25 ≈ 510 MPa. It is higher than the ideal σ̄ ln R because of friction and redundant work.

questions.q: Wire drawing 3 → 2.5 mm, σ̄ 400 MPa: ideal drawing stress
questions.why: The ideal drawing stress is σ_d = σ̄ ln(A₀/A) = 400 × ln(3²/2.5²) = 400 × ln 1.44 = 400 × 0.365 ≈ 146 MPa.

questions.q: Milling MRR: w 60, d 3, f_m 300 mm/min
questions.why: MRR = w × d × feed rate = 60 × 3 × 300 = 54 000 mm³/min. Divide by 60 for mm³/s: 900 mm³/s.

questions.q: Merchant: α 15°, μ 0.7 (β ≈ 35°): φ
questions.why: By Merchant's relation, φ = 45° + α/2 − β/2 = 45 + 7.5 − 17.5 = 35°, using β = tan⁻¹(0.7) ≈ 35°.

questions.q: Max reduction per pass (ideal) in drawing
questions.why: The ideal drawing stress cannot exceed the flow stress, so ln(A₀/A) ≤ 1 and A₀/A ≤ e. The maximum reduction in area is 1 − 1/e ≈ 63%.
